meta.blurb: A dirty, tired seventeen-year-old walks into Philadelphia with almost no money, buys three rolls and is laughed at by a girl who will become his wife. Benjamin Franklin tells the rest himself, from his thirteen virtues to the clubs he founded.
meta.bible: Benjamin Franklin: born in Boston in January 1706, died in 1790 aged 84; printer, writer, inventor, public servant; the author, who wrote the book in parts in 1771, 1784 and 1788 and left it unfinished. William Franklin: his son, to whom the first part is addressed as Dear Son. Josiah Franklin: his father, a Candle and Soap maker from Ecton in Northamptonshire. Abiah Folger: his mother. James Franklin: his older brother, a printer, who made Benjamin his apprentice at twelve. John Collins: a boyhood friend. Matthew Adams: a bookseller's customer who lent him books. Silence Dogood: the made-up widow in whose name Benjamin wrote letters to his brother's newspaper. Samuel Keimer: a printer in Philadelphia. Sir William Keith: the governor of Pennsylvania, who promised letters of credit and sent none. James Ralph: a friend who sailed with him to London. Thomas Denham: a kind Quaker merchant. Hugh Meredith: his first business partner. Deborah Read: his wife from 1730. Joseph Breintnall, Thomas Godfrey, Robert Grace, William Coleman: members of the Junto, the club of friends. George Whitefield: the preacher of 1739. Dr Thomas Bond: his friend who began the hospital. General Edward Braddock: the British commander of 1755. Pennsylvania Gazette: his newspaper from 1729. Poor Richard: the Almanack he published from 1732. Library Company: the first subscription library, 1731. Pilgrim's Progress, Plutarch's Lives, The Spectator, Xenophon: books and writers he read. The thirteen virtues: Temperance, Silence, Order, Resolution, Frugality, Industry, Sincerity, Justice, Moderation, Cleanliness, Tranquillity, Chastity, Humility. Places: Boston, Ecton, New York, Perth Amboy, Burlington, Philadelphia, London, Pennsylvania, Albany, Lancaster, Twyford, Delaware, Market Street. Key terms: Apprentice, Tallow, Almanack, Printing press, Newspaper, Vegetarian, Junto, Subscription, Militia, Lightning, Dissertation, Indenture, Sloop. Added for the full-length book (200 beats, 20 chapters, kept in the order of Franklin's own account, from the Twyford letter of 1771 to his sailing for England in 1757): Twyford: the English country house where he began the book in 1771. Thomas Franklin: his uncle, a smith and public-spirited scrivener of Ecton. Benjamin Franklin the elder: his uncle, a silk dyer and writer of shorthand poems and sermons, who gave him his name. Queen Mary: in whose reign the family hid an English Bible under a joint stool. Peter Folger: Abiah's father, an early settler of Nantucket. Samuel Franklin: a cousin, a cutler in Boston. George Brownell: the schoolmaster who taught him writing. John Bunyan, Richard Burton, Daniel Defoe, Cotton Mather, Plutarch, Cocker, Seller, Sturmy, John Locke, Xenophon, Socrates, Thomas Tryon, Pope, Greenwood: authors he read. Blackbeard: the pirate of his sailor's song. The Lighthouse Tragedy: his ballad. The Spectator: the magazine he copied. New-England Courant: James's newspaper of 1721. Harvard: the college mocked by Silence Dogood. Andrew Bradford, William Bradford: the two printers, son in Philadelphia and father in New York. Amboy, Burlington, Long Island, Cooper, Schuylkill, Chestnut, Market Street: places on the way. Dr Brown: a travelling doctor and friend. Charles Osborne, Joseph Watson: friends in Philadelphia. Robert Holmes: his brother-in-law, a sloop captain. Colonel French: with Governor Keith. William Burnet: Governor of New York. John Franklin: his brother in Newport. Vernon: whose debt Benjamin collected. Little Britain, Bartholomew Close, Palmer, Watts, Lincoln's Inn Fields, Wild Court, Cheapside, Bloomsbury, Chelsea, Blackfriars, Thames, Gravesend, Berkshire: London places and ships. Wollaston: author of The Religion of Nature. Lyons, Mandeville, Pemberton, Sir Isaac Newton, Sir Hans Sloane, Sir William Wyndham: people of London. Water-American: his nickname among the pressmen. Aquila Rose: a dead friend of Keimer's. Stephen Potts, George Webb, David Harry: Keimer's workmen. George House: who brought the first customer. Nicholas Scull, William Parsons, William Maugridge, Thomas Godfrey: Junto members. Dr Baird: who praised his industry. Brockden: the scrivener who drew up the library's articles. Richard Saunders: the made-up author of Poor Richard. Titan Leeds: a rival Almanack maker. Samuel Hemphill: a young preacher from Ireland. Abel James, Benjamin Vaughan: friends whose letters led him to resume the book at Passy in 1784. Colonel Spotswood: the postmaster-general of 1737. Whitefield: George Whitefield, the preacher; Georgia: where he built an orphan house. Christ. Thomas: the Governor who offered a patent for the stove. Lawrence, Clinton, Allen: leaders of the Association of 1747, and the Governor of New York who lent eighteen cannon. Thomas Penn: one of the Proprietors. David Hall: his partner from 1748. Dr Spence: who showed him electricity in Boston in 1746. Peter Collinson: the London friend who sent a glass tube. Ebenezer Kinnersley: who lectured on electricity. Dalibard: the Frenchman who drew sparks from a rod in 1752. Royal Society, Copley, Fellow: the Society that gave him its medal in 1753. Yale: the college that gave him a degree. William Hunter: joint postmaster-general from 1753. James Alexander, Kennedy: New Yorkers who approved his Albany plan. Six Nations, Lords of Trade, Board of Trade, President General, Grand Council: of the Albany plan of 1754. Morris: Governor Robert Hunter Morris. Frederick: the Maryland camp. Fort Duquesne, Monongahela, Dunbar, St Clair, Shirley, Braddock: the campaign of 1755. Gnadenhutten, Bethlehem, Moravian, Fort Allen: the frontier in 1756. Clapham, Beatty, Denny: the colonel who took over, the army chaplain, and the Governor of 1756. Loudoun, Innis: the commander-in-chief and a messenger. Falmouth, Scilly: where he landed in England in July 1757. Key terms: Smallpox, Inoculation, Asbestos, Pleurisy, Copperplate, Gruel, Presbyterian, Postmaster, Electricity, Lightning, Pamphlet, Sermon, Almanack, Contributionship. Voice and tone: first person told simply in third person for learners, warm, wry and honest; Franklin laughs at his own faults; the writer admires his curiosity and his habit of improving himself.

beats.scene: A white-haired man writes at a desk in a quiet English country house
beats.summary: In the summer of 1771 Franklin, staying at a country house in England, begins to write his life as a letter to his son William.

beats.scene: An old man smiles as he writes about his family's past
beats.summary: Franklin explains that old men like to tell of the past, that his family may enjoy it, and that he would gladly live his life again, correcting its mistakes like a printer.

beats.scene: A small stone village with a church and farms in the English countryside
beats.summary: Franklin traces his family to Ecton, where they farmed about thirty acres for roughly three hundred years and the eldest son was always the smith.

beats.scene: A village blacksmith talks with neighbours in a busy country lane
beats.summary: Franklin learned the family stories from his uncle Thomas, a clever blacksmith who helped the whole village and died four years to the day before Benjamin was born.

beats.scene: A child keeps watch at a door while a family reads a hidden Bible
beats.summary: In Queen Mary's reign the family hid an English Bible under a stool, and a child watched the door while it was read aloud.

beats.scene: An old man writes small signs in a notebook beside a curious boy
beats.summary: Uncle Benjamin, a silk dyer from London, moved to Boston in old age, wrote poems and sermons in shorthand, and the boy was named after him.

beats.scene: A family with trunks boards a sailing ship bound for America
beats.summary: About 1682 Josiah, a dyer whose church was forbidden, sails to Boston with his wife and three children, and there takes up candle and soap making.

beats.scene: A man plays the violin and sings while neighbours listen
beats.summary: Josiah is strong, clever with his hands, plays the violin and sings, and his neighbours come to him for advice.

beats.scene: A woman serves a large family at a long table in Boston
beats.summary: Josiah's second wife was Abiah Folger, daughter of an early settler of Nantucket, and between the two marriages he had seventeen children.

beats.scene: Boston roofs and a church tower under a winter sky in 1706
beats.summary: Benjamin is born in Boston in January 1706, the youngest son of a crowded family.

beats.scene: A small boy reads a book beside a tall church window
beats.summary: Josiah meant to give his youngest son to the Church; Benjamin learned to read very early and could not remember being taught.

beats.scene: A boy in a Latin schoolroom stands first among his classmates
beats.summary: At eight Benjamin goes to grammar school, rises to the top of his class, and is moved up a year; then his father takes him out because the cost is too high.

beats.scene: A teacher guides a boy's hand as he writes in a plain schoolroom
beats.summary: Benjamin moves to Mr Brownell's school, learns to write well but fails at arithmetic, and leaves school at ten.

beats.scene: A boy in an apron cuts thread for candle wicks in a busy workshop
beats.summary: At ten Benjamin works in his father's shop, cutting wicks, filling moulds, running errands, and he hates the work.

beats.scene: A boy swims in a pond while other boys wait on the shore
beats.summary: Benjamin loves the water, swims well, learns to manage boats and canoes, and often leads the other boys.

beats.scene: Boys carry stones to build a small wharf beside a muddy pond
beats.summary: Benjamin and his friends take building stones to make a wharf by a marsh; the workmen find them out, and his father teaches him that nothing is useful which is not honest.

beats.scene: A father walks with his son past a busy carpenter's workshop
beats.summary: Josiah takes Benjamin around Boston to watch joiners, bricklayers, turners and brass workers so that he may choose a trade; he learns to use tools.

beats.scene: Two cousins stand at a grinding wheel in a cutler's shop
beats.summary: Benjamin is tried for a short time at his cousin Samuel's cutlery shop, but the fee is too high and he returns to the candles.

beats.scene: A father talks with friends at a long table while a boy listens
beats.summary: At Josiah's table the talk was of things that were good, just or wise; Benjamin paid so little heed to his food that he scarcely knew what he ate.

beats.scene: A boy sells his small toys at a counter and buys little books
beats.summary: Benjamin spends every penny he earns on books, reads whatever he can find, and becomes a lover of reading.

beats.scene: A boy reads beside a shelf of thick old books in a small library
beats.summary: His father's small library holds mostly books of religious argument, which Benjamin reads, and later he thinks the time might have been better spent.

beats.scene: A boy swaps a pile of small books for another heap at a stall
beats.summary: He loves Bunyan's stories, sells them to buy Burton's Historical Collections, a set of small cheap books of history and travel.

beats.scene: A young man studies two books beside a window at dusk
beats.summary: He reads Defoe's Essay on Projects and Cotton Mather's Essays to Do Good, which shape his thinking about helping others.

beats.scene: A young man walks home from the harbour while the brothers talk
beats.summary: James, Benjamin's older brother, returns from England in 1717 with a printing press and type, and opens a print shop in Boston.

beats.scene: A boy of twelve signs a paper beside a wooden printing press
beats.summary: At twelve Benjamin signs a paper that binds him as an apprentice to James until he is twenty-one, with wages only in the last year.

beats.scene: A boy hands back a borrowed book at dawn at a bookseller's door
beats.summary: Benjamin becomes skilful; he borrows books from booksellers' boys and from Matthew Adams, reading at night and returning them clean by morning.

beats.scene: A young poet sings a ballad in the street to a small crowd
beats.summary: He writes two ballads, The Lighthouse Tragedy and a song about the pirate Blackbeard, and sells them in the streets, pleased with his success.

beats.scene: A father reads his son's verses with a shake of his head
beats.summary: Josiah laughs at the poems and tells him that makers of verses are generally beggars, so Benjamin gives up poetry and turns to prose.

beats.scene: Two boys argue at a table while a father reads papers by candlelight
beats.summary: In letters with his friend John Collins on whether women should be educated, Benjamin argues the other side; his father reads them and points out faults in his spelling and style.

beats.scene: A teenage boy finds a volume of The Spectator in a bookshop
beats.summary: Benjamin finds a volume of The Spectator, reads it again and again, and longs to write as well.

beats.scene: A teenage boy copies out a magazine essay by candlelight at night
beats.summary: He makes short notes of each essay, sets them aside, then tries to write the essay again from his notes and compares it to the original, finding his faults.

beats.scene: A young man arranges slips of paper in a different order on a desk
beats.summary: To gain words and order, he turns tales into verse and back to prose, and he jumbles his notes and tries to put them in the best order before comparing; sometimes his is better.

beats.scene: A young man studies a book of numbers at a printing desk
beats.summary: At sixteen he masters Cocker's arithmetic by himself and reads two books on navigation, learning a little geometry.

beats.scene: A young man reads a thick book on thinking at a table
beats.summary: He reads Locke on human understanding and a French book on the art of thinking, and learns that careful reasoning can be a pleasure.

beats.scene: A young man questions an older friend politely in a quiet room
beats.summary: Reading about Socrates, he gives up blunt arguing and takes up asking humble questions that lead others to see where they are wrong.

beats.scene: A young man speaks gently to a friend over a small table
beats.summary: He adopts a gentler style, saying I think rather than certainly, and finds that others accept his views more easily.

beats.scene: A young man in a print shop reads a book while eating plain bread
beats.summary: At sixteen he reads a book by Tryon on vegetable diet and decides to stop eating meat, which makes problems for his brother's household.

beats.scene: A young man eats bread and raisins at a printing desk while others leave
beats.summary: He offers James half of what is paid for his board, saves the money for books, and eats biscuit and raisins while the others go out to eat, using the time to study.

beats.scene: A cod fish fries in a pan on a small boat deck
beats.summary: Later, on a voyage, the smell of fried cod tempts him; he notices smaller fish inside and decides that, if fish eat one another, he may eat them, and he eats meat again.

beats.scene: A young man carries bundles of newspapers through morning streets
beats.summary: In 1721 James starts a newspaper, the New-England Courant; some of his friends say one is enough, but he goes ahead, and Benjamin carries the papers to customers.

beats.scene: A young man pushes a folded letter under a printing-house door at night
beats.summary: Longing to write, but sure his brother would refuse a boy's writing, Benjamin disguises his hand and slips letters under the print-house door at night.

beats.scene: Men gather in a print shop and read a letter aloud with smiles
beats.summary: The friends praise the piece and guess who the writer is; Benjamin hears them name learned men and feels proud.

beats.scene: A countrywoman in a plain dress sits writing a letter at a desk
beats.summary: Writing as Silence Dogood, a clergyman's widow from the country, he sends fourteen letters about the follies of the town, and the paper's readers enjoy them.

beats.scene: James frowns at his younger brother across a print shop
beats.summary: When the secret comes out, James is cross and jealous; he thinks the praise has made Benjamin vain.

beats.scene: A teenage boy stands before stern men in dark coats in a council room
beats.summary: The brothers disagree often, James sometimes beats him, and Benjamin feels that this harsh treatment makes him hate arbitrary power.

beats.scene: A man sits in a prison cell while a boy works the press alone
beats.summary: James criticises the government in his paper and is jailed for a month in 1722; Benjamin is questioned by the council but let go, and he runs the paper alone meanwhile.

beats.scene: Men in black coats hand a paper to James in front of a press
beats.summary: Early in 1723 the Assembly orders that James may no longer print the Courant; his friends decide it should appear under Benjamin's name, and the old agreement is cancelled so that the boy is free.

beats.scene: Two brothers argue in a print shop and one raises his hand
beats.summary: Benjamin knows James would not dare to show the secret agreement, so when the quarrels return and James strikes him, he takes his freedom; he later called it unfair.

beats.scene: A young man hurries past a closed print shop with his bag
beats.summary: James tells the Boston printers not to employ him, and his father sides with James, so Benjamin decides to leave Boston; his friend John Collins helps him find a place on a sloop.

beats.scene: A small sailing boat leaves Boston harbour at dawn with a young passenger
beats.summary: Benjamin tells the captain a story to explain why he must leave quietly, boards the sloop, and in three days arrives in New York, at seventeen, three hundred miles from home with no friends.

beats.scene: A young man asks an old printer for work in a New York shop
beats.summary: In New York the printer William Bradford has no work but sends Benjamin to his son Andrew in Philadelphia, a hundred miles away.

beats.scene: A small boat is tossed by a storm while a man falls overboard
beats.summary: Crossing the bay, a squall tears the sail and a drunken Dutchman falls overboard; Benjamin pulls him out by the hair, and the man's wet book is a Dutch Pilgrim's Progress.

beats.scene: A small boat anchors off a stormy shore at night with soaked passengers
beats.summary: Driven toward Long Island, the boat cannot land through the surf, so the passengers anchor for a cold night; Benjamin gets a fever and cures it by drinking much water and sweating.

beats.scene: A young man walks through heavy rain on a country road
beats.summary: From Amboy he walks toward Burlington in the pouring rain, is taken for a runaway servant at an inn, and befriends a travelling doctor named Brown.

beats.scene: An old woman serves a hot dinner to a tired young man
beats.summary: At Burlington he misses the regular boat, an old woman who sells gingerbread feeds him and lets him wait, and a boat at last comes by and he rows through the night.

beats.scene: A dirty, tired young man steps off a boat onto a wharf
beats.summary: On a Sunday morning in October 1723 he lands at Market Street wharf, dirty, with his pockets stuffed, and buys three large puffy rolls.

beats.scene: A man with a roll under each arm passes a girl at a door
beats.summary: He walks up Market Street eating a roll with one under each arm, and Deborah Read, standing at her father's door, thinks he looks ridiculous; he gives the spare rolls to a woman and child.

beats.scene: A young man sleeps on a bench in a silent meeting house
beats.summary: He follows well-dressed people into a Quaker meeting house, sits among the silent worshippers and falls asleep until someone wakes him; it is the first house he sleeps in at Philadelphia.

beats.scene: A young printer eats breakfast at a table with an older printer
beats.summary: He goes to Andrew Bradford, who gives him breakfast but has no work and sends him to a new printer, Keimer; Bradford's father, who rode ahead on horseback, takes him there.

beats.scene: A thin man sets type straight from his head at an old press
beats.summary: Keimer's shop has a crazy old press and one set of worn type; he is composing a poem on the death of Aquila Rose straight into type; Benjamin mends the press, prints the poem and gets work and a room at Mr Read's.

beats.scene: Four young men talk about books on a riverbank near Philadelphia
beats.summary: He makes friends with young readers, Charles Osborne, Joseph Watson and James Ralph, and on Sundays they walk by the Schuylkill River and read to each other.

beats.scene: A thin man with a long beard stands beside an old printing press
beats.summary: Keimer wears a long beard, keeps Saturday as his day of rest, and loves religious argument; Benjamin puzzles him with Socratic questions, and Keimer proposes founding a new sect with Benjamin as preacher.

beats.scene: A thin man eyes a roast pig on a table while guests wait
beats.summary: Benjamin agrees to Keimer's rules if Keimer gives up meat; they live on vegetables for three months, and then Keimer, tempted by a roast pig ordered for guests, eats it all himself.

beats.scene: A gentleman in a long coat visits a small print shop
beats.summary: Benjamin's brother-in-law, Captain Holmes, shows Governor Keith a letter from Benjamin; Keith, impressed, visits the shop in person with Colonel French and takes Benjamin to a tavern to taste Madeira wine.

beats.scene: A governor and a young printer talk over a table with wine
beats.summary: Keith says the printers of the town are poor, promises him the public printing, and gives him a letter for his father; Benjamin takes a boat to Boston in April 1724.

beats.scene: A young man in a fine new suit arrives at his father's door
beats.summary: After seven months away he surprises his family in a fine suit with a watch and nearly five pounds in silver; all welcome him but James, who is offended when Benjamin shows his money and gives the workmen a coin to drink.

beats.scene: A father reads the governor's letter while his son waits nervously
beats.summary: Josiah reads Keith's letter and thinks him foolish to back an eighteen-year-old; he refuses the money but blesses his son, warns him against insulting others in print, and promises help if he saves until twenty-one.

beats.scene: Two young men sail into Newport harbour on a small boat
beats.summary: On the way back he visits his brother John in Newport, where a friend, Mr Vernon, asks him to collect a debt of about thirty-five pounds in Pennsylvania.

beats.scene: A governor in a wig shows his library to a young traveller
beats.summary: At New York the sloop's captain tells Governor Burnet about a passenger with many books; Burnet shows him his library and talks with him kindly.

beats.scene: Two young men struggle in a rowing boat on a river
beats.summary: Collins takes to drink and gambling and borrows Benjamin's money, including some of Vernon's; on the river he is too drunk to row and Benjamin tips him overboard; he never repays.

beats.scene: A governor shakes hands with a young printer in a fine room
beats.summary: Back in Philadelphia, Keith offers to send Benjamin to London to buy a press, with letters of credit; Benjamin and Deborah Read agree with her mother that any marriage must wait.

beats.scene: A ship at sea in winter with two young men and a Quaker merchant
beats.summary: In November 1724 Benjamin and Ralph sail for London; the governor's letters are said to be in the mail bag, but when the bag is searched in the Channel none is for Benjamin.

beats.scene: A kind merchant explains something to a surprised young man in a London street
beats.summary: In London, Denham tells him Keith has no credit and makes promises he cannot keep; Benjamin sees he gave hopes because he had little else to give; he and Ralph rent a cheap room in Little Britain.

beats.scene: A poor young poet reads his verses to a friend in a small room
beats.summary: Ralph will not go home or take plain work; he tries to be an actor and then a poet, and Benjamin lends him about twenty-seven pounds he never gets back.

beats.scene: A young printer sets type in a crowded London printing house
beats.summary: At Palmer's printing house he sets type for Wollaston's The Religion of Nature, disagrees with its arguments, and prints a few copies of his own pamphlet, which he later counts as a mistake.

beats.scene: A clever surgeon and a famous author talk at a crowded London tavern
beats.summary: Through a surgeon named Lyons he meets Dr Mandeville at a tavern in Cheapside; Pemberton promises an introduction to Sir Isaac Newton that never happens; Sir Hans Sloane buys his asbestos purse.

beats.scene: A young man writes one short letter at a table in a London room
beats.summary: Busy with work, plays and friends, he lets his feeling for Deborah fade and writes to her only once; he later calls it one of the great mistakes of his life.

beats.scene: A strong young man carries two heavy forms of type up the stairs
beats.summary: At Watts's large printing house he works at the press, carries a form of type in each hand, and drinks water while the others drink beer, so they call him the Water-American; he argues that bread gives more strength than beer.

beats.scene: Printers crowd round a young man at a long table in a composing room
beats.summary: In the composing room the men demand five shillings as a welcome fee, which he has already paid in the press room; after weeks of tricks blamed on the chapel ghost, he pays, having learned that it is foolish to be on bad terms with those one lives with.

beats.scene: A man floats in the Thames near a bridge while men watch from boats
beats.summary: He swims from Chelsea to Blackfriars with a friend, doing tricks on and under the water, and Sir William Wyndham asks him to teach his sons, so he thinks of opening a swimming school.

beats.scene: A kind merchant shows a young man a list of goods in an office
beats.summary: After about eighteen months Denham, about to return to Philadelphia, offers Benjamin work as his clerk at fifty pounds a year, promising to teach him accounts and set him up later; Benjamin accepts.

beats.scene: A young man writes in a journal on the deck of a ship
beats.summary: The Berkshire sails from Gravesend in July 1726; Benjamin keeps a journal and, at sea, writes a plan for conducting his future life, which he keeps to faithfully into old age.

beats.scene: A young man walks along the Philadelphia waterfront and passes an older man
beats.summary: He lands at Philadelphia on 11 October 1726; Keith is no longer governor and passes him in the street, ashamed; Deborah has married a potter named Rogers but soon parted from him.

beats.scene: Shelves of goods in a busy Philadelphia store with a Quaker merchant
beats.summary: In Denham's store in Water Street Benjamin learns accounts and trade, lodges with Denham, and is advised by him like a son.

beats.scene: Two sick men lie in a quiet room while a doctor watches
beats.summary: In early 1727 both fall ill; Benjamin nearly dies of pleurisy and is almost sorry to recover; Denham dies after a long illness, leaving him a small gift in his will.

beats.scene: A young man returns to a cluttered print shop full of untrained workers
beats.summary: Alone again, he returns to Keimer, who offers a large wage to manage the shop and teach his untrained workers, including Meredith, Potts and Webb, though Keimer plans to dismiss him once they have learned.

beats.scene: A young man pours melted metal into a small mould to make letters
beats.summary: There is no type foundry in America, so Benjamin makes a mould and strikes new matrices from the old letters; he also engraves, makes the ink and keeps the warehouse, a real factotum.

beats.scene: A young man turns away from his shouting master in the street
beats.summary: Keimer shouts at him from the street before the neighbours; Benjamin walks out, and Meredith, whose father has money, proposes a partnership; they send to London for a press and type.

beats.scene: A copperplate press stands in a Burlington room with printed banknotes
beats.summary: Keimer sends a civil message asking him back to print New Jersey's paper money; Benjamin builds the first copperplate press in the country, cuts the ornaments, and impresses the leading men of Burlington.

beats.scene: Two young men set up a new press while a countryman pays
beats.summary: The press arrives, and Franklin and Meredith rent a house near the market; George House brings a countryman who wants a printer, and his five shillings are their first earnings, giving Franklin more pleasure than any crown since.

beats.scene: Young tradesmen in leather aprons gather around a table in a tavern
beats.summary: In the autumn of 1727 Franklin forms the Junto, a club of clever friends who meet on Friday evenings to discuss morals, politics and natural science.

beats.scene: Ten friends with different trades sit together reading at a long table
beats.summary: The members include Breintnall, Godfrey, Scull, Parsons, Maugridge, Meredith, Potts, Webb, Grace and Coleman.

beats.scene: A member reads an essay aloud while others listen with pens in hand
beats.summary: Each member brings questions and reads an essay every three months; debates are held in a spirit of inquiry, and direct contradiction is forbidden under small fines.

beats.scene: Members hand a job order to a young printer across a desk
beats.summary: The Junto lasts many years and is the best school of philosophy, morals and politics in the province; members help one another, and Breintnall wins Franklin forty sheets of Quaker history to print.

beats.scene: Two printers glare at each other across a street over newspapers
beats.summary: Franklin plans a newspaper and confides in George Webb, who tells Keimer; Keimer announces a paper of his own, with Webb as his helper.

beats.scene: A busy man in a coat sits writing essays at a printing-shop desk
beats.summary: To keep readers from Keimer's paper, Franklin and Breintnall write funny Busy-Body essays for Bradford's; Keimer's paper limps on with ninety subscribers and he sells it to Franklin, who makes it the Pennsylvania Gazette.

beats.scene: A man reads a newspaper aloud to a group of Assembly members
beats.summary: Franklin makes the Gazette much better; his lively remarks on the quarrel between Governor Burnet and the Massachusetts Assembly are talked about, and the leading men become subscribers.

beats.scene: Merchants and farmers argue about coins and paper notes over a table
beats.summary: In 1729 the people want more paper money and the rich oppose it; Franklin writes a pamphlet in its favour, the Assembly votes the money, and his friends reward him with the job of printing it.

beats.scene: A tired young man hands a bundle of papers to a quiet partner
beats.summary: Meredith is often drunk and his father cannot pay his share, so the partners are sued; Coleman and Grace each offer to lend Franklin money to take over alone, and Meredith leaves for North Carolina.

beats.scene: A young printer works by lamplight while neighbours pass the window
beats.summary: A form of type breaks apart and Franklin sets it again before bed; Dr Baird tells a merchants' club that he sees Franklin working late and early, and Franklin even wheels paper home on a barrow, so his credit grows.

beats.scene: A young printer and Deborah Read stand together in a small room
beats.summary: Deborah's husband Rogers has gone to the West Indies and is rumoured to have had another wife and died; no one can prove it, and Benjamin and Deborah marry on 1 September 1730.

beats.scene: A woman folds and stitches pamphlets in a small shop while a boy plays
beats.summary: Deborah proves a faithful helper, tending the shop, stitching pamphlets and buying old linen rags for the paper makers; they live thriftily and William grows up in the household.

beats.scene: A man finds a china bowl and a silver spoon on his breakfast table
beats.summary: Franklin eats bread and milk from a cheap bowl until one morning Deborah surprises him with a china bowl and silver spoon costing twenty-three shillings; luxury enters the house.

beats.scene: Friends carry books into a small room and place them on shelves
beats.summary: The Junto's shared books scatter, so in 1731 Franklin proposes a subscription library: fifty members pay forty shillings and then ten shillings a year, and Brockden draws up the articles.

beats.scene: A young printer asks a man to join a library, saying friends sent him
beats.summary: Franklin presents the library as the wish of a number of friends rather than his own idea, and finds it works so well that he uses the method ever after.

beats.scene: Farmers and shopkeepers read quietly in a small library room by lamplight
beats.summary: The library gives Franklin the means of constant study, for which he sets aside an hour or two each day, and he thinks such libraries made Americans better informed and readier to defend their rights.

beats.scene: Two friends play chess while an open book lies between them
beats.summary: Franklin teaches himself French, then Italian and Spanish; with a friend learning Italian, he plays chess, and the winner sets the loser a task in the language.

beats.scene: A young man reads a Latin book beside a window in the evening
beats.summary: He looks at Latin again and finds he can read it easily, and suggests that students should learn the modern languages before the ancient ones.

beats.scene: Two brothers shake hands beside a sick man's bed in Newport
beats.summary: Around 1733 Franklin visits Boston and stops at Newport, where he and the ill James are reconciled; James asks him to bring up his ten-year-old son as a printer, and he does.

beats.scene: A father sits sadly beside a small empty bed
beats.summary: In 1736 Franklin's son Francis, aged four, dies of smallpox; Franklin regrets that he had not inoculated him and tells the story for the sake of other parents.

beats.scene: A printer at a desk writes jokes and sayings for an Almanack
beats.summary: In 1732 Franklin begins Poor Richard's Almanack under the name Richard Saunders, full of amusing and useful matter; he continues it for about twenty-five years and sells nearly ten thousand a year.

beats.scene: A farmer reads a proverb in an Almanack by a candle
beats.summary: In the spaces of the calendar Franklin prints sayings that urge industry and thrift, such as the hard-to-stand empty sack and early to bed and early to rise.

beats.scene: An old Almanack maker looks angrily at a younger printer
beats.summary: Poor Richard predicts the death of a rival Almanack maker, Titan Leeds; when Leeds protests that he is alive, Poor Richard replies that a ghost must be writing in his name.

beats.scene: A tall old man gives a speech to a crowd at an auction
beats.summary: For the Almanack of 1758 Franklin gathers all Poor Richard's sayings into one speech by a wise old man at an auction; it is copied in every newspaper and printed in Britain and France.

beats.scene: A man sits quietly at a plain wooden table with an open book
beats.summary: Franklin holds a few simple beliefs: that one God made and governs the world, that the best service to God is doing good to people, that the soul is immortal, and that virtue is rewarded.

beats.scene: A young preacher speaks from a pulpit to a puzzled crowd
beats.summary: A young preacher, Mr Hemphill, teaches morals rather than doctrine; Franklin writes pamphlets in his defence, but when one sermon is shown to be copied he gives up the cause and uses his Sundays for study.

beats.scene: An old man in a French house reads letters from two friends
beats.summary: Years later, urged by friends Abel James and Benjamin Vaughan to continue his life story, Franklin takes up the book again in 1784 at Passy in France.

beats.scene: A young man writes a bold plan in a notebook by candlelight
beats.summary: Around 1730 he forms the bold and difficult project of arriving at moral perfection, living without any fault, and finds it harder than he had imagined.

beats.scene: A list of twelve words is written in neat columns in a small book
beats.summary: He decides good habits must be built first, and lists twelve virtues, each with a short rule: temperance, silence, order, resolution, frugality, industry, sincerity, justice, moderation, cleanliness, tranquillity and chastity.

beats.scene: A neat notebook with red lines and small black marks lies beside a pen
beats.summary: He keeps a little book with a page for each virtue and a column for each day, marks every fault with a black spot, and gives one week's strict attention to each virtue in turn, four courses a year.

beats.scene: A man writes a daily timetable on a page by candlelight
beats.summary: Each morning he asks what good he will do that day, each evening what good he has done; his day runs from rising at five to bed at ten, with work, reading, music and conversation.

beats.scene: A man sits quietly at a table, eating little and listening to others
beats.summary: Temperance comes first because it brings a cool and clear head, and silence second, because he wishes to learn by listening and to break a habit of prattling, punning and joking.

beats.scene: A neat desk with papers in order beside a man holding a speckled axe
beats.summary: Order is the hardest virtue for him; he tells of a man who wanted his whole axe polished bright, tired of turning the wheel, and decided that he liked a speckled axe best.

beats.scene: A young printer works quietly in a tidy shop with a ledger and tools
beats.summary: Resolution, frugality and industry have plain rules; he hopes frugality and industry will free him from debt and bring independence, making sincerity and justice easier to practise.

beats.scene: A quiet Quaker friend speaks gently to a young man in a shop
beats.summary: A Quaker friend tells him people think him proud, so he adds humility as a thirteenth virtue with the rule to imitate Jesus and Socrates, and he stops using words of certainty.

beats.scene: A man bows his head slightly while another speaks with confidence
beats.summary: Pride is the hardest passion to subdue; even if he thought he had beaten it he would probably be proud of his humility, but his modest manner helps him carry his points though he is a poor speaker.

beats.scene: An old man looks at a small notebook full of faint marks
beats.summary: Franklin never reached perfection, but the attempt made him a better and happier man; he credits temperance with his health, industry and frugality with his fortune, and sincerity and justice with his country's trust, and hopes his descendants follow.

beats.scene: A man plans a book at a desk with a quill and loose pages
beats.summary: He plans a book, The Art of Virtue, to show that wrong actions are forbidden because they are harmful, and dreams of a united party of good people in every nation, but public and private business prevent him from finishing either.

beats.scene: A printer turns away a customer who holds out an angry pamphlet
beats.summary: Franklin keeps libel and personal abuse out of his newspaper, offering to print such pieces separately; he explains in an essay of 1731 that printers believe both sides deserve a hearing and that truth beats error in fair play.

beats.scene: A printer hands a sealed letter to a young journeyman heading south
beats.summary: Franklin helps several workmen open print shops in other colonies for a third of the profits over six years; in Charleston a partner dies and his widow, trained in Holland, sends exact accounts every quarter and later buys the shop.

beats.scene: A clerk writes in a large book while Assembly members talk behind him
beats.summary: In 1736 Franklin is chosen clerk of the Assembly and is re-elected for several years; the post helps him keep friends among the members and brings the printing of the colony's votes, laws and paper money.

beats.scene: A man returns a borrowed book to an Assembly member with a smile
beats.summary: Rather than flatter his opponent, Franklin asks to borrow a scarce book from his library and returns it a week later with warm thanks; the man becomes a friend for life, proving that one who has done you a kindness will do you another.

beats.scene: A post rider rides away on a horse with a bag of letters
beats.summary: In 1737 Colonel Spotswood, the postmaster-general, takes the Philadelphia post from Bradford for poor accounts and offers it to Franklin, who finds it helps his newspaper and income.

beats.scene: A post rider hands newspapers to a printer while a rival glares
beats.summary: Bradford, when postmaster, had forbidden his riders to carry Franklin's paper, which Franklin had to get round by bribing them; Franklin thought it mean and did not do the same to Bradford.

beats.scene: A vast crowd stands in a Philadelphia street listening to a preacher
beats.summary: In 1739 the travelling preacher George Whitefield arrives; when the clergy refuse him their pulpits he preaches in the fields to huge crowds, and the whole town seems to grow religious.

beats.scene: A man walks backward down a street, listening to a distant voice
beats.summary: Franklin walks backward down Market Street to learn how far Whitefield's voice carries, and calculates that more than thirty thousand could hear him, which makes the old tales of generals addressing armies believable.

beats.scene: A man reaches into his pocket as a collection plate is passed
beats.summary: Franklin resolves to give nothing to Whitefield's orphan-house collection, but as the sermon goes on he gives first his coppers, then his silver, and finally empties his pocket of gold.

beats.scene: A guest at a printer's table accepts a bed from his host
beats.summary: When Whitefield returns Franklin offers him a bed, and the preacher says he will be rewarded if it is for Christ's sake; Franklin replies that it is for Whitefield's sake; the two keep a sincere civil friendship until Whitefield's death.

beats.scene: A preacher and a printer look at plans for a large building
beats.summary: Franklin thinks the orphan house should be built in Philadelphia rather than Georgia, where costs are greater; Whitefield refuses to change, so Franklin gives nothing, though he prints many of the preacher's sermons and journals.

beats.scene: A man listens carefully to a preacher who speaks every word clearly
beats.summary: Franklin notes that Whitefield's delivery improved with repetition until every accent and pause was perfect, like fine music, though his printed works were less impressive.

beats.scene: Neighbours pass leather buckets along a line toward a burning house
beats.summary: In 1735 Franklin writes that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and in 1736 forms the Union Fire Company of thirty men, each keeping leather buckets, strong bags and baskets ready and meeting monthly.

beats.scene: Several fire companies gather with ladders and buckets in a busy street
beats.summary: So many men want to join that new companies are formed one after another, until they include most men of property, and in 1752 Franklin and fellow members found a company to insure houses against fire.

beats.scene: A night watchman with a lantern walks a quiet street at midnight
beats.summary: The city watch is weak: householders are meant to take turns, but constables excuse them for a yearly fee that goes on drink, and the fee is unfair to the poor; Franklin writes a paper proposing paid watchmen and a property tax.

beats.scene: Members of several clubs listen to a proposal in a crowded tavern room
beats.summary: The Junto approves the plan and Franklin passes it to other clubs formed by its members, each proposing it as its own idea; a few years later it becomes law.

beats.scene: A farmer's wagon is stuck in thick mud in a Philadelphia market street
beats.summary: Streets are unpaved and the market is a quagmire in wet weather; Franklin persuades neighbours to pay for paving one part of the market place with stone, which helps until mud from unpaved lanes dirties it again.

beats.scene: A poor man sweeps a paved street in the morning while shopkeepers watch
beats.summary: Franklin finds a poor industrious man to sweep the pavement for sixpence a month from each household, and prints a paper showing how cheap it is and how much dust it saves in shops and houses; the plan works and is later extended by law.

beats.scene: A lamplighter lifts a ladder beside a smoky lamp at night
beats.summary: The first street lamps are globes from London that blacken with smoke; Franklin designs lamps with four flat panes, a funnel above and air holes below, which burn bright until morning and are easily mended.

beats.scene: An old man writes thoughtfully beside a window above a clean street
beats.summary: Franklin admits that some will call these matters trifles, but says that human happiness comes less from great strokes of fortune than from small daily advantages, and that teaching a poor young man to shave may do more good than a gift of a thousand guineas.

beats.scene: Curious men gather around a table with maps, instruments and letters
beats.summary: In 1743 Franklin proposes a society of curious people to share discoveries; it is called the American Philosophical Society, and he serves as its secretary; it fades but is later revived and still exists.

beats.scene: A man pours coals into an iron stove while a family warms their hands
beats.summary: In 1742 Franklin invents an open iron stove that warms rooms better and saves fuel by warming the fresh air; his friend Robert Grace casts the plates; when Governor Thomas offers a patent, Franklin refuses on principle.

beats.scene: Enemy ships on the horizon of a harbour as anxious townspeople watch
beats.summary: When war with France and Spain threatens the Delaware, Philadelphia has no forts, guns or soldiers, because the Quaker-led Assembly will not vote money for war.

beats.scene: A printer works late on a pamphlet as printed sheets dry on a line
beats.summary: In November 1747 he writes and prints Plain Truth, which paints the town's defenceless state in strong terms, argues for union and discipline, and promises a plan for an association to sign; it has a sudden and surprising effect.

beats.scene: A crowd packs a large hall to sign a paper at tables
beats.summary: At a meeting in the New Building Franklin hands out printed papers with pens and ink; over twelve hundred sign at once and in the end more than ten thousand, who arm themselves, form regiments and drill weekly.

beats.scene: A man in plain clothes declines a sword offered by an officer
beats.summary: The Philadelphia regiment elects Franklin colonel, but he declines as unfit and recommends Mr Lawrence, a man of influence; Franklin proposes a lottery to pay for a battery of guns below the town.

beats.scene: Four gentlemen dine with a governor at a table full of wine
beats.summary: Franklin and three others are sent to New York to borrow cannon from Governor Clinton, who refuses at first, but at a dinner with plenty of Madeira he offers six, then ten, and finally eighteen.

beats.scene: Volunteers drag heavy cannon on carriages toward a river battery
beats.summary: The cannon are fine eighteen-pounders; they are carried to the battery, where the volunteers keep a nightly guard while the war lasts, and Franklin takes his turn as a common soldier.

beats.scene: A man draws flags with bold pictures and short mottoes at a table
beats.summary: Franklin devises the pictures and mottoes for the flags of the companies; the governor and council are glad, but Thomas Penn, one of the Proprietors, thinks Franklin has too much influence over the people.

beats.scene: Soldiers hang up muskets as townspeople celebrate peace in the street
beats.summary: Peace comes in 1748 and the Association fades away; it has shown that ordinary citizens can unite to protect themselves when government will not act, and it makes Franklin a leader the people trust and the Proprietors watch.

beats.scene: A man in a judge's chair looks puzzled at a thick law book
beats.summary: The governor makes Franklin a justice of the peace; he attends the courts a few times, finds he lacks knowledge of the common law, and gradually withdraws, excusing himself as busy in the Assembly.

beats.scene: Two printers shake hands over a ledger in a busy print shop
beats.summary: In 1748 Franklin takes David Hall, a skilled and honest workman, into partnership; Hall runs the shop and pays Franklin his share of the profits for eighteen years, giving Franklin leisure for study.

beats.scene: A lecturer shows glowing sparks from a glass tube to a puzzled audience
beats.summary: In 1746 in Boston Franklin sees Dr Spence's electrical experiments, imperfectly done but wholly new to him, and they both surprise and please him.

beats.scene: A glass tube lies on a library table beside a curious crowd
beats.summary: Soon after, the Library Company receives from Peter Collinson in London a glass tube with directions; Franklin repeats what he saw, practises, adds new experiments, and his house is full of visitors.

beats.scene: Friends gather around a table as a young man lectures with a glass tube
beats.summary: To share the labour Franklin has glass tubes made for friends; Ebenezer Kinnersley, an out-of-work neighbour, lectures for money using lectures Franklin writes, and later tours the colonies.

beats.scene: Friends dine beside a river while sparks fly from a glass jar
beats.summary: In a funny letter of 1749 Franklin describes a picnic by the Schuylkill where a turkey is to be killed by an electric shock and roasted on a spit turned by electricity.

beats.scene: A man holds a pointed iron rod near a charged ball
beats.summary: Franklin finds that electricity acts like one fluid, positive when in excess and negative when short, and that a pointed metal rod draws off sparks; he suspects lightning is electricity and that a rod could protect buildings.

beats.scene: Scientists in Paris watch an iron rod rise into a thunderstorm
beats.summary: The Royal Society thinks his letters hardly worth printing, but Collinson publishes them as a book and a French translation brings fame; in May 1752 near Paris Dalibard draws sparks from a rod in a storm as Franklin proposed.

beats.scene: A man and his son fly a kite under a dark thundercloud
beats.summary: According to the famous account, in June 1752 Franklin flies a kite in a storm near Philadelphia and draws a spark from a key on the wet string; he promotes the lightning rod, which soon protects many buildings.

beats.scene: A scholar in a gown receives a gold medal at a long table
beats.summary: In 1753 the Royal Society gives Franklin its gold medal and Harvard and Yale each give him a master's degree; he takes no patent on any invention and the Royal Society later makes him a Fellow without fees.

beats.scene: A printer hands out copies of a pamphlet about schools to gentlemen
beats.summary: In 1749 Franklin writes Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pennsylvania and gives copies free to leading citizens, then opens a subscription for an academy, to be paid over five years; he does not present it as his own idea.

beats.scene: Boys and teachers fill a large hall for the first lessons
beats.summary: The Academy opens in 1751 in the great hall built for Whitefield, whose trustees agree to its use; twenty-four trustees from different churches govern it, Franklin writes its rules, and it grows into the University of Pennsylvania.

beats.scene: A doctor speaks earnestly to a printer about a house for the sick poor
beats.summary: Dr Thomas Bond proposes a hospital for the sick poor but finds little support; rich men keep asking whether Franklin has been consulted, so Bond comes to him.

beats.scene: A printer writes an article about the hospital beside a stack of newspapers
beats.summary: Franklin asks Bond to explain the plan, subscribes himself, and first prepares the public by writing about hospitals in the newspaper, as he usually does, a step Bond had left out.

beats.scene: Assembly members argue as a clerk reads out a bill about money
beats.summary: The country members of the Assembly oppose paying for a city hospital, so Franklin proposes a bill giving two thousand pounds once private citizens raise the same; both sides support it, and he excuses his small cunning.

beats.scene: Builders lay the first stone of a large brick hospital
beats.summary: Subscriptions soon pass the needed sum, the managers claim the public gift, the Pennsylvania Hospital opens in a rented house in 1752, and in 1755 the cornerstone of its building is laid with words by Franklin; it still serves patients today.

beats.scene: A man in a plain coat is sworn in at an Assembly hall
beats.summary: In 1751 Franklin is elected to the Assembly and is re-elected for many years; in 1753 he becomes joint postmaster-general of the colonies with William Hunter, and the post office soon makes a profit for the Crown.

beats.scene: A traveller on horseback rides through a forest toward a council fire
beats.summary: In 1754, with war against France near, the Lords of Trade call the colonies to meet the Six Nations at Albany; Franklin is a Pennsylvania commissioner and on the way drafts a plan to unite the colonies, which friends in New York approve.

beats.scene: A snake cut into pieces, each labelled with a colony's initials
beats.summary: In May 1754 Franklin prints in his Gazette a picture of a snake cut into eight pieces, each marked with a colony, over the words Join, or Die, often called the first political cartoon in America.

beats.scene: Delegates sit around a long table at Albany with a map
beats.summary: Franklin's plan proposes a general government under a President General appointed by the Crown and a Grand Council chosen by the colonial assemblies; after daily debate at Albany it is agreed and sent to the Board of Trade and the assemblies.

beats.scene: Two letters are refused in separate rooms, one in London and one in Philadelphia
beats.summary: The plan fails: the assemblies reject it as giving the Crown too much power and the Crown rejects it as giving the people too much; Franklin believes it was the true middle way and that it might have prevented the later quarrel and war.

beats.scene: A governor and a printer talk over dinner after a heated debate
beats.summary: Governor Morris, bound by the Proprietors' instructions not to let their estates be taxed, quarrels with the Assembly; Franklin writes many of its replies, yet the lively governor bears him no ill will and invites him to dine.

beats.scene: An army camp with red-coated soldiers and a postmaster arriving on horseback
beats.summary: In spring 1755 General Braddock arrives in Virginia with two regiments to take Fort Duquesne; he waits at Frederick for wagons and is angry with Pennsylvania's Assembly, which sends Franklin with his son William to smooth things over.

beats.scene: A general and a postmaster talk in a tent while soldiers wait outside
beats.summary: Braddock says Maryland and Virginia have sent few usable wagons; Franklin says nearly every Pennsylvania farmer owns a wagon, and Braddock asks him to find them; Franklin writes the terms and a commission is prepared on the spot.

beats.scene: A notice on a board in Lancaster is read by farmers beside their horses
beats.summary: At Lancaster Franklin publishes a notice that a hundred and fifty wagons and fifteen hundred pack horses are wanted at good daily pay, warning that Sir John St Clair might otherwise come with soldiers and take them by force.

beats.scene: A long line of farm wagons with horses stands on a dusty road
beats.summary: The farmers do not trust the army, so Franklin pledges his own bond for their pay; he advances Braddock's money and then some of his own, and in about two weeks a hundred and fifty wagons and 259 pack horses are on their way.

beats.scene: Twenty parcels of food and wine are tied onto horses outside a house
beats.summary: Franklin learns that the army's young officers are poor, and persuades a committee of the Assembly to pay for twenty parcels of tea, sugar, coffee, cheese, ham and wine, each on its own horse; William leads the train, and Braddock thanks and repays him.

beats.scene: A soldier in a red coat speaks proudly while a printer listens with worry
beats.summary: Franklin warns Braddock that his four-mile line of march might be cut like a thread by an ambush; Braddock smiles and replies that such enemies may frighten raw militia but cannot harm trained regulars, and Franklin says no more.

beats.scene: Soldiers flee a smoky forest while a wounded general lies in a wagon
beats.summary: On 9 July 1755 the army is ambushed near Fort Duquesne and defeated; Braddock dies of his wounds, and Colonel Dunbar destroys stores and hurries back toward Philadelphia, leaving the frontier open.

beats.scene: Farmers crowd around a worried printer holding a paper bond
beats.summary: The owners of the lost wagons and horses demand payment under Franklin's bond, claims so large he could never pay; General Shirley, who has taken command, appoints commissioners to examine them and most are paid from the army's funds.

beats.scene: Assembly members debate a militia bill at a long table
beats.summary: With the frontier exposed, Franklin writes a bill for a voluntary militia that leaves the Quakers at liberty, and a dialogue answering all objections to it; he thinks it has a great effect.

beats.scene: A burned settlement with smoke on the horizon and a messenger on horseback
beats.summary: In late 1755 raids kill settlers and the Moravian mission at Gnadenhutten is destroyed; Governor Morris asks Franklin to defend the north-west frontier and build forts, and, though no soldier, he accepts, raising about five hundred and sixty men with William as aide.

beats.scene: A stone town with a stockade and women ready with stones at high windows
beats.summary: At Bethlehem, the chief Moravian town, Franklin finds a good defence: a stockade, arms bought from New York, and small paving stones set between the upper windows for the women to throw down on any attackers.

beats.scene: Soldiers fell tall pine trees and set them upright to form a fort
beats.summary: At Gnadenhutten Franklin's men fell pines, raise a stockade and mount one swivel gun, firing it to show the enemy they have such pieces; the miserable stockade, Fort Allen, is finished in about a week despite hard rain.

beats.scene: Soldiers gather around a minister who hands out rum after prayers
beats.summary: Franklin notices men are content when busy and quarrelsome when idle; the chaplain Mr Beatty complains that few attend prayers although all come for their rum, so Franklin suggests he deal out the rum after prayers, and attendance becomes perfect.

beats.scene: A man hands over command to an officer while soldiers stand in a line
beats.summary: Colonel Clapham, an experienced officer, arrives at the forts and Franklin hands over the command; back in Philadelphia the regiment has elected him colonel, and its mounted officers meet him with drawn swords, which offends the Proprietors' friends.

beats.scene: A new governor presents a gold medal to a calm printer at a dinner
beats.summary: In August 1756 Governor Denny presents Franklin with the Royal Society's gold medal at a public dinner, then privately hints that the Proprietors will reward him if he stops opposing them; Franklin says he needs no favours.

beats.scene: Assembly members vote to send a petition across the sea
beats.summary: The quarrel over taxing the Proprietors' estates goes on until the Assembly resolves to petition the King and in 1757 chooses Franklin as its agent to carry the complaint to London; he accepts.

beats.scene: A busy general in a New York office with petitioners waiting
beats.summary: In spring 1757 Franklin goes to New York to take the mail ship; Lord Loudoun, the commander-in-chief, is slow to finish his letters, and each day he is told they will be ready tomorrow.

beats.scene: A tired messenger sits in an anteroom while a general delays
beats.summary: In the waiting room Franklin meets a messenger named Innis, kept waiting for weeks, who says Loudoun is like St George on a tavern sign, always on horseback and never riding on.

beats.scene: A mail ship runs before the wind past rocky cliffs in the mist
beats.summary: At last in June 1757 Franklin sails from New York for England; near the end of the voyage the ship passes dangerously close to rocks in the dark, but escapes and lands at Falmouth in July.

beats.scene: An old man with white hair sits at a desk among papers
beats.summary: The book stops in 1757; Franklin lived until 1790 and helped to shape a new nation, but he left his own story unfinished.

He believed in God, and he believed in doing good.

A widow in Carolina kept very clear accounts for him.

He borrowed a book, and an enemy became a friend.

When Franklin ran the mail, he was fair to Bradford.

Franklin walked away to test how far his voice carried.
Franklin gave away all his money after the sermon.
They were friends, although they believed different things.

Whitefield spoke clearly, and it sounded like music.
He and his friends made a team to fight fires.

His club passed the idea to other clubs.

A poor man swept the street for a small fee.
Franklin made new lamps that stayed bright all night.
He said that small things can make people happy.

They chose Franklin as a leader, but he said no.

Franklin joked that a turkey could be cooked by a spark.
He found that sparks and lightning are alike.
Scientists in France proved that Franklin was right.
He flew a kite in a storm to catch lightning.
Famous colleges and societies gave him special honours.
He wrote a plan for a new school in Philadelphia.
In 1751, the new school opened its doors.
Doctor Bond wanted a hospital, but few people helped.
Franklin wrote about the hospital in his newspaper.
Franklin made a clever plan to help raise money.
The new hospital opened and helped many sick people.
In 1751, Franklin joined the Assembly of Pennsylvania.
In 1754, Franklin traveled to Albany to meet leaders.
His picture of a cut snake asked the colonies to unite.
The delegates at Albany agreed to Franklin's plan.
The plan failed, and Franklin was sad about it.
Governor Morris argued with Franklin but stayed friendly.
In 1755, General Braddock came to fight the French.
Franklin said that Pennsylvania's farmers had many wagons.
He told farmers to rent wagons and horses to the army.
Franklin promised to pay farmers, so many farmers came.
He sent food and drink as gifts to the officers.
Franklin warned the general, but he did not listen.
In July 1755, Braddock's army lost the battle.
Farmers asked Franklin to pay for their lost wagons.

B1B2: In the summer of 1771, Benjamin Franklin was staying in a quiet English country house. There he began a long letter to his son William about his own life.

Franklin said that old men like to talk about the past, and he hoped his family would enjoy his story. He added that if he could live again, he would ask only to correct his mistakes, as a printer does.

Franklin's family had lived for about three hundred years in Ecton, a village in Northamptonshire, where they farmed a small piece of land. The eldest son was always trained as the village blacksmith, and the name Franklin once meant a free landowner.
Franklin's uncle Thomas was a clever blacksmith who helped his neighbours and served the whole village. He died four years to the day before Benjamin was born.
In the days of Queen Mary, reading the English Bible could bring trouble. Franklin's great-great-grandfather hid it under a stool, and a child watched the door while he read.
Franklin's uncle Benjamin had been a silk dyer in London before he moved to Boston in his old age. He wrote poems, taught himself a kind of shorthand, and gave the boy his name.
Josiah Franklin worshipped in a way that English law forbade, and his meetings were often disturbed. About 1682 he sailed to Boston with his wife and three children, hoping to pray in freedom.
Josiah Franklin was a strong man with a sound mind and clever hands. In the evenings he played the violin and sang, and his neighbours often came to ask for his advice.
Josiah's second wife, Abiah Folger, was the daughter of an early settler on the island of Nantucket. She was a sensible woman, and she fed her large family well.
Benjamin was born in Boston in January 1706, the youngest son of the family. At times thirteen children sat down together at Josiah's table.
Josiah decided to give his youngest son to the Church, as a kind of gift from the family. Benjamin learned to read so early that he could not remember being taught.

At the age of eight, Benjamin was sent to the Boston grammar school, where he quickly rose to the top of his class. His father soon changed his mind, because the school cost a great deal and few of its students became rich.
Benjamin then went to a school where Mr Brownell taught writing and arithmetic. He learned to write well, but he failed in arithmetic, and at ten years old he left school for good.
In his father's shop Benjamin cut the wicks for candles, filled the moulds and ran errands around the town. He disliked the work, and he began to dream of life at sea.
Benjamin loved the water, and he learned to swim and to handle a boat. When he was with other boys, he was usually the leader.
Near the mill pond there was a muddy marsh where the boys liked to fish. To build a wharf, Benjamin and his friends took stones meant for a new house, and the workmen found out.

To find a trade that his son would like, Josiah took Benjamin around Boston to watch carpenters, bricklayers and metal workers. Benjamin enjoyed seeing skilled hands at work, and he learned to use tools himself.
Benjamin's father thought of making him a cutler, who makes knives, and sent him to his cousin Samuel's shop for a trial. Samuel wanted a fee that Josiah thought too high, so the boy came home again.

Josiah liked to talk with his guests about useful and interesting subjects, and he steered the conversation to things that were good. Benjamin listened so closely that, even years later, he hardly knew what he had eaten.
As a boy, Benjamin spent every penny that he earned on books. He read whatever he could find, and by the age of twelve he was a great lover of reading.
Josiah kept a small library, and most of its books were about religious arguments. Benjamin read many of them, though later he thought his time might have been better spent.
Benjamin first loved the stories of John Bunyan, such as Pilgrim's Progress. He later sold them in order to buy a set of small, cheap history books.
Two books, Defoe's Essay on Projects and Mather's Essays to Do Good, made a deep impression on him. They gave him a way of thinking that influenced some of the main events of his later life.
Benjamin's older brother James had learned the printing trade in England. In 1717 he came back to Boston with a press and a set of type, and he opened a print shop.
At twelve years old, Benjamin signed a contract to serve his brother as an apprentice until he was twenty-one. He would receive wages only in the last year.

As an apprentice, Benjamin made quick progress and soon knew the trade well. He borrowed books from a kind customer named Matthew Adams and read them at night, so that he could return them clean in the morning.

Benjamin tried to write poetry, and he wrote two songs which his brother had him sell in the streets. One was about a lighthouse accident, and the other was about the capture of the pirate Blackbeard.
Josiah made fun of the songs and told his son that poets are usually beggars. So Benjamin was saved from becoming a poor poet, and he turned his attention to writing in prose.

Benjamin wrote letters to his friend John Collins about whether girls should be educated, and he argued the opposite side for fun. His father found the papers and told him that his style was weaker than his friend's.
Around this time, Benjamin came across an odd volume of The Spectator, a famous magazine of essays. He had never seen it before, and he read it over and over with delight.

To learn the Spectator's style, Benjamin made short notes about each essay and put them aside for several days. Then he tried to write the essay again in his own words and compared it with the original, correcting his faults.
To learn more words, Benjamin turned stories into poems and then back into prose. He also mixed up his notes and put them in order again, and sometimes his order was better.
At sixteen, Benjamin picked up a book of arithmetic, and he worked through the whole thing alone with great ease. He also read two books on navigation, and he learned a little geometry from them.
Benjamin also read Locke's famous book about the human mind and a French book called The Art of Thinking. These books taught him how to reason with care and to use clear words.
From a book about the Greek thinker Socrates, Benjamin learned to ask polite questions instead of arguing. He found that people changed their minds more easily when he drew them toward the answer.
Benjamin gave up words such as certainly and undoubtedly, and he said I think or I imagine instead. He found that people listened more kindly and gave way more easily.
When he was sixteen, Benjamin read a book by Thomas Tryon that recommended eating only vegetables. He decided to give up meat, though this caused some trouble in his brother's household.

Benjamin told James that he would buy his own food if James gave him half of the board money. With the money he saved he bought books, and while the others went out to dinner he read in the empty shop.
Later, on a ship, Benjamin smelled fried cod and found it hard to resist. He saw small fish inside the cod, and he decided that if fish ate one another, he could eat them too.

In 1721, James began a newspaper, the New-England Courant, which was the second in America. His friends said that one newspaper was enough for the colonies, but James went ahead, and Benjamin delivered the copies.

Benjamin longed to write for the paper, but he knew that James would never print a young apprentice's work. So he disguised his handwriting and slipped an essay under the printing-house door at night.
James's friends read the essay aloud, and they praised it warmly. Benjamin listened while they guessed at the author, and they named only clever and learned men.

Benjamin invented a countrywoman named Silence Dogood, who was a minister's widow, and he wrote fourteen letters in her name. The letters were about the follies of the town, and readers enjoyed them very much.
At last Benjamin told his brother who had written the letters. James was not pleased, and he thought the praise would make the boy too proud.
The brothers began to quarrel often, and James sometimes struck Benjamin. He felt that his brother was harsh and unfair, and he grew to hate the rule of one man over another.

In 1722, James printed an article that angered the government, and the Assembly sent him to jail for a month. Benjamin was also questioned, but he said nothing, and the council let him go because he was only an apprentice.
In January 1723, the Assembly said that James must not print the Courant any more. His friends put the paper under Benjamin's name, so James gave back the boy's apprenticeship papers.
Soon the brothers quarrelled again, and James struck Benjamin. Benjamin knew that James would not dare to show the secret agreement, so he left, though he later felt this was not fair.
James spoke to the other printers in Boston, and none would hire Benjamin. His father also took James's side, so Benjamin decided to leave town secretly.

Benjamin gave the captain a story to explain why he had to leave in secret, and the sloop sailed from Boston. In three days he reached New York, three hundred miles from home, without a friend in the place.
In New York, the old printer William Bradford had no work for Benjamin. He said that his son Andrew in Philadelphia, a hundred miles away, might need a helper.
A sudden storm tore the boat's sail as it crossed the bay. A drunk Dutchman fell into the water, but Benjamin caught his hair and pulled him back on board.
The wind drove the boat toward Long Island, where the waves were too high for a landing. The passengers spent a cold, wet night at anchor, with almost nothing to eat or drink.

From Amboy, Benjamin walked toward Burlington in the pouring rain, and by evening he was soaked. At a small inn, people suspected that he was a runaway servant, but a friendly doctor named Brown talked with him about books.
In Burlington, Benjamin missed the boat, but a kind old woman gave him dinner and let him wait. When another boat came by, there was no wind, so everyone rowed all night.
On Sunday morning Benjamin stepped onto the wharf in Philadelphia, dirty and very tired. He had only a Dutch dollar and some copper coins, and with a little of it he bought three large rolls.
Benjamin walked up Market Street with a roll under each arm, eating the third. At her father's door stood a young woman, Deborah Read, who thought he looked very funny.
Benjamin followed some well-dressed people into a Quaker meeting, where everyone sat in silence. He was so tired that he fell asleep, and a kind person woke him when it ended.
Andrew Bradford gave Benjamin breakfast but had no work for him. His father, who had ridden from New York, took the young man to see a new printer named Keimer.
Keimer's print shop was poor, with a broken old press and a small set of worn type. Benjamin mended the press, printed his poem, and was given a job and a room at Mr Read's house.
In Philadelphia, Benjamin made friends with three young readers named Osborne, Watson and Ralph. On Sundays they walked in the woods by the Schuylkill River and read to each other.
Keimer wore a long beard and kept Saturday as his holy day. He loved to argue about religion, and he wanted to start a new church with Benjamin as its preacher.
Benjamin agreed to Keimer's rules if Keimer would stop eating meat for a while. After three months Keimer ordered a roast pig, and he could not wait, so he ate it all himself.
Sir William Keith, the governor, read a letter that Benjamin had written and was very impressed. He came to the print shop in person, to the surprise of Keimer, and asked Benjamin to dine with him.

At the tavern, Keith said that Philadelphia's printers were poor and that Benjamin could easily do better. He promised him the government's printing, and he wrote a letter to Benjamin's father asking for help.
Benjamin returned to Boston in a new suit, with a watch and nearly five pounds in silver. At the print shop he showed the workers his money and gave them a coin to drink, which made James furious.
Josiah read the governor's letter and decided that Keith was foolish to trust a boy of eighteen. He refused the money, but he promised to help if Benjamin saved carefully until he was twenty-one.
On the way back, Benjamin visited his brother John in Newport. A friend of John's, Mr Vernon, asked him to collect a debt of about thirty-five pounds in Pennsylvania.
In New York, the captain told Governor Burnet about a passenger who owned many books. The governor invited Benjamin to see his large library and talked with him about authors.
In New York, Collins began to drink and gamble, and he soon borrowed Benjamin's money. On the river he was too drunk to row, so Benjamin tipped him into the water.
Governor Keith said he would send Benjamin to London to buy a press and type. He promised letters that would give Benjamin the money he needed there.
In November 1724, Benjamin sailed for London with his friend Ralph. The captain said the governor's letters were in the mail bag, but when it was opened, there were none for Benjamin.
In London, Mr Denham told Benjamin that the governor had no credit at all. Keith liked to please everyone, and since he had little to give, he gave people hopes instead.
James Ralph did not want a plain job, and he would not return to America. He tried to become an actor and then a poet, while Benjamin paid his bills.
Benjamin worked at Palmer's, a famous London printing house, and set the type for a book about religion. Some of its ideas seemed weak to him, so he wrote a short reply and printed a few copies.
In London, Benjamin met some famous writers and thinkers. He sold a purse made of asbestos, a stone cloth that fire cannot burn, to the collector Sir Hans Sloane.
In London, Benjamin almost forgot about Deborah Read, and he wrote her only one letter. He said later that this was one of the great mistakes of his life.
At Watts's big printing house, the workers drank beer all day. Benjamin drank only water, and he could carry two heavy forms of type at once, so they called him the Water-American.
The compositors asked Benjamin for five shillings as a welcome gift, but he had already paid in the press room. He refused for weeks, until the tricks played on him forced him to pay.
Benjamin swam a long way down the Thames, from Chelsea to Blackfriars, doing tricks on the way. A nobleman, Sir William Wyndham, heard of it and asked him to teach his sons.
Mr Denham planned to return to Philadelphia and open a store. He offered Benjamin a job as his clerk, and Benjamin, who was tired of London, said yes.
The ship Berkshire left Gravesend in July 1726, and Benjamin kept a journal of the voyage. In it he wrote a plan for his future life, and he kept to it faithfully until he was old.
Benjamin landed at Philadelphia on 11 October 1726 and found that many things had changed. Sir William Keith was no longer governor, and Deborah Read had married a potter named Rogers.
In Water Street, Denham and Benjamin opened a store and lived together. Denham advised him like a father, and Benjamin respected and loved him.
In February 1727, both Denham and Benjamin fell seriously ill. Benjamin nearly died of pleurisy, but he recovered, while Denham grew worse and died, leaving him a small gift.
Keimer offered Benjamin a good wage to manage his printing house and teach his new workers. Benjamin guessed that Keimer meant to dismiss him as soon as they had learned.
There was no type foundry in America, so Benjamin made his own letters with a mould that he invented. He also made the ink and worked as a warehouseman.
One day Keimer shouted at Benjamin in front of all the neighbours. Benjamin put on his hat and walked out, and Hugh Meredith offered to start a business with him.
Keimer needed Benjamin to print the paper money of New Jersey, so he sent a polite message. Benjamin built a copperplate press for the job, the first in the country.

Benjamin and Hugh Meredith opened their print shop when the new press arrived from London. Their first customer paid five shillings, and the money pleased Benjamin more than any crown he earned later.
In the autumn of 1727, Benjamin gathered his clever friends into a club that he called the Junto. They met on Friday evenings to talk about ideas and to help each other improve.
The first members included a shoemaker, a surveyor, a joiner and a mathematician. Franklin praised the young gentleman Robert Grace for his generosity, and William Coleman for his clear head.
