Each member had to bring a question to discuss and read an essay of his own every three months. Direct contradiction was forbidden, and anyone who broke the rule paid a small fine.
The Junto lasted for many years, and it was a fine school of ideas for the town. Its members also helped each other, and Breintnall found a large printing job for Franklin and Meredith.
Benjamin planned to start his own newspaper, but he told the secret to George Webb. Webb told Keimer, who quickly announced a newspaper of his own.

To spoil Keimer's plan, Franklin and Breintnall wrote funny essays called the Busy-Body for Bradford's paper. Keimer's own paper had only about ninety readers, so he sold it to Franklin for a small sum.

Franklin's paper was much better than Keimer's had been. His clever remarks on a quarrel between Governor Burnet and the Massachusetts Assembly were talked about, and soon the leading people were subscribers.
In 1729 many people wanted more paper money, and Franklin wrote a pamphlet that supported them. The Assembly agreed, and as a reward Franklin was given the profitable job of printing the new money.
Hugh Meredith drank too much, and his father could not pay his share of the debts. Two friends, Coleman and Grace, each offered to lend Benjamin money to take over the business alone.
One night a form of type fell apart, and Franklin set it again before he went to bed. Neighbours saw his hard work, and a respected man said that he was always working when others were asleep.
Deborah's husband Rogers had gone to the West Indies, and people said he was dead or had another wife. Nobody could prove it, but Benjamin and Deborah decided to marry on 1 September 1730.
Deborah proved to be a faithful and hard-working wife. She tended the shop, folded and stitched pamphlets, and bought old rags for the paper makers.
Franklin liked a simple breakfast of bread and milk, which he ate from a cheap earthen bowl. One morning he found a china bowl and a silver spoon, which Deborah had bought for twenty-three shillings.
Franklin's friends brought books to the Junto, but the shared collection did not last long. In 1731 he proposed a library paid for by its members, each of whom would pay a fee to join.
When Franklin asked people to join the library, he said it was the plan of a group of friends. He found that people supported a plan more happily when he did not seek the credit.
The new library gave Franklin the chance to study a little each day. He believed that such libraries made ordinary tradesmen and farmers as intelligent as gentlemen in other countries.
Franklin taught himself French, and then Italian and Spanish. A friend who also studied Italian played chess with him, and the winner gave the loser a lesson to learn.
After French, Italian and Spanish, Franklin found that he could read Latin with surprising ease. He thought that students should begin with the modern languages and then move to the ancient ones.
Around 1733, Benjamin visited Boston and then went to see his brother James in Newport. The brothers made peace, and James, who was ill, asked Benjamin to train his young son as a printer.
In 1736, Franklin's little son Francis died of smallpox at the age of four. He always regretted not protecting the boy by inoculation, and he told the story to warn other parents.
In 1732, Franklin began to publish an Almanack under the name of Richard Saunders. He tried to make it both fun and useful, and it sold about ten thousand copies each year.

Franklin filled the spaces in the calendar with short sayings about hard work and thrift. One of them said that it is hard for an empty sack to stand upright, because a poor man finds it hard to be honest.
Poor Richard predicted that a rival Almanack maker, Titan Leeds, would die on a certain day. Leeds protested that he was alive, but Poor Richard answered that a ghost was writing in his name.
In 1757, Franklin gathered the best sayings of Poor Richard into a speech by a wise old man at an auction. The piece was copied by newspapers across America and was printed in Britain and in France.
Franklin never doubted that God made the world and governed it. He believed that the best way to serve God was to do good to other people.

A young preacher named Hemphill taught good behaviour more than church rules, and Franklin wrote pamphlets in his defence. When someone found that one of his sermons was copied from another writer, Franklin stopped supporting him.
Years later, two friends wrote to Franklin and urged him to continue his life story. In 1784, while living in France near Paris, he began to write again.

Around 1730, Franklin formed a bold plan to become morally perfect and never to commit a single fault. He soon found it harder than he had imagined, because bad habits returned whenever he stopped paying attention.
Franklin decided that good wishes were not enough, and that he must form good habits. He wrote a list of twelve virtues, and he gave each virtue a short rule.
Franklin kept a little book with a page for each virtue. Each week he watched one virtue closely, and he marked a small black spot for every fault.
Each morning Franklin asked himself what good he would do that day. Each evening he asked what good he had done, and he kept a plan for his hours of work, reading and rest.
Franklin put temperance first, because a clear head helps with every other virtue. He put silence next, because he wanted to learn by listening and to stop idle chatter and jokes.
Order was the virtue that Franklin found hardest to keep, because he was always busy. He told a story of a man who wanted his axe polished all over, then chose a speckled one.
Franklin wrote a short rule for each virtue, such as lose no time and waste nothing. He hoped that frugality and industry would free him from debt and bring him wealth and independence.

A Quaker friend told Franklin kindly that people thought him proud, so he added a thirteenth virtue, humility. His rule was to imitate Jesus and Socrates, and he stopped using positive, forceful words.
Franklin said that no natural feeling is harder to defeat than pride. Even if he had overcome it, he joked, he would probably be proud of his humility.
Franklin never reached perfection, but he believed that trying made him a better and happier man. He thanked temperance for his good health, and industry and frugality for his early comfort.
Franklin planned to write a book called The Art of Virtue, but he never found the time. He argued that bad actions are not wrong because they are forbidden, but forbidden because they are harmful.

Franklin refused to print insults and attacks on people in his newspaper. If someone insisted, he offered to print the piece separately, but he would not use his subscribers' paper for private quarrels.

Franklin helped several of his workmen to start print shops in other colonies, sharing the profits. One widow in Charleston, who had learned bookkeeping as a girl in Holland, sent him clear accounts every quarter.

In 1736, Franklin was chosen to be clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly, and he was chosen again each year. The job paid well and helped him keep friends among the members, which brought him printing work.
Franklin asked his opponent to lend him a rare book, and the man did so at once. After Franklin returned it with warm thanks, the two became friends for life.
In 1737, the head of the colonial post offered Franklin the job of postmaster in Philadelphia. The salary was small, but the job helped his newspaper to get news and to reach more readers.

When Bradford was postmaster, he forbade the riders to carry Franklin's newspaper, so Franklin had to bribe them. When Franklin took over the office, he thought it mean to treat Bradford the same way, and he did not.

In 1739 the preacher George Whitefield came to Philadelphia, and when the churches closed their doors to him, he spoke outdoors. Huge crowds of all churches came to hear him, and Franklin was one of them.

One evening Franklin walked backward down Market Street to see how far Whitefield's voice would carry. By measuring the space around him, he decided that more than thirty thousand people could hear the preacher.
Franklin decided that he would give nothing when the preacher asked for money. As the sermon went on, however, he gave first his coppers, then his silver, and at last his gold.
Franklin offered Whitefield a bed in his house, and Whitefield said that God would reward him. Franklin answered that he had offered it not for Christ's sake but for Whitefield's.
Franklin thought that the orphan house should be built in Philadelphia, not in Georgia, where building would cost much more. Whitefield refused to change his plan, so Franklin would not give money.
Franklin noticed that Whitefield's sermons improved because he had repeated them so often. Every pause and every tone of his voice was so perfect that listening was like hearing fine music.
In 1735, Franklin wrote that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. He then formed a fire company of thirty men, and each promised to keep leather buckets and strong bags ready.
So many men wanted to join that new fire companies were formed, one after another. Years later, in 1752, Franklin and his fire-company friends also started a company to insure houses against fire.

Franklin saw that the night watch was weak, because the constables took fees and spent them on drink. He wrote a paper proposing paid watchmen and a tax that depended on how much property each person owned.
The Junto liked the plan for the watch, and Franklin passed it to other clubs that its members had started. Each club proposed it as its own idea, and some years later it became law.
In wet weather, Market Street was a sea of mud, and wagons sank into it. Franklin helped to raise money to pave one stretch of the market with stone.

Franklin found a poor, hard-working man who would sweep the street in front of the houses for sixpence a month from each family. He wrote a paper that showed how dust ruined goods in shops, and how cheap the remedy was.
The first street lamps were round glass globes, which turned black with smoke in a few hours. Franklin designed a lamp with four flat panes and a chimney on top, and it stayed bright until morning.
Franklin knew that some readers would call these things trifles. But he believed that happiness comes less from great luck than from the small comforts that people enjoy every day.
In 1743 Franklin proposed a club where curious people in the colonies could share what they learned. It was called the American Philosophical Society, and Franklin was its secretary.
In 1742 Franklin invented an iron stove that warmed rooms better and used less wood. The governor offered him a patent so that he alone could sell it, but Franklin refused.
In 1744, Britain went to war with France and Spain, and enemy ships appeared near Philadelphia. The town had no defence, because the Quakers who led the Assembly would not pay for war.
Franklin wrote and printed a pamphlet called Plain Truth. It showed how defenceless the city was and promised a plan for ordinary people to defend themselves.
Franklin called a meeting in a big hall, and he handed out copies of his paper with pens and ink. More than twelve hundred people signed at once, and in the end over ten thousand signed.
The men of Philadelphia chose Franklin as their colonel, but he declined, saying he was no soldier. He suggested Mr Lawrence, a man of influence, and Lawrence was appointed.
Governor Clinton of New York refused at first to lend the cannon. At dinner, with plenty of Madeira wine, he offered six, then ten, and finally eighteen.
The eighteen cannon were fine guns, and the volunteers carried them to the battery. They kept a nightly guard while the war lasted, and Franklin took his turn like everyone else.

Franklin also designed pictures and mottoes for the flags of the companies. The governor and his council were pleased, but the Proprietor, Thomas Penn, thought Franklin had too much power over the people.
The war ended in 1748, and the volunteer companies stopped meeting. The Association had shown that ordinary citizens can unite to protect themselves when the government will not act.
The governor made Franklin a justice of the peace, a kind of local judge. He found that he did not know enough law for the job, so he gradually withdrew from it.
In 1748, Franklin made David Hall his partner, and Hall took over the work of the print shop. For eighteen years he paid Franklin his share of the profits, and Franklin enjoyed more free time.
In 1746, in Boston, Franklin saw some electrical experiments by a Scottish visitor, Dr Spence. They were not well done, but the subject was so new that they surprised and pleased him.
Peter Collinson, a friend in London, sent the Library Company a glass tube and some instructions. Franklin repeated the experiments he had seen, and after much practice he added new ones.
To share the work, Franklin had more glass tubes made for his friends. One of them, Ebenezer Kinnersley, gave public lectures for money, and Franklin wrote the lectures for him.
In 1749 Franklin wrote a funny letter about a picnic by the Schuylkill River. At the picnic, he joked, a turkey would be killed by an electric shock and cooked using electricity.

Franklin discovered that an electric charge can be positive or negative, and that a pointed metal rod can draw off a spark. He began to think that lightning might be a huge electric spark, which a pointed rod could lead safely away.
Franklin's letters were printed in London, and a French translation reached Paris. In May 1752, French scientists tested his idea with an iron rod during a storm, and it worked.
According to the famous story, Franklin flew a kite in a thunderstorm in 1752. A spark jumped from a key tied to the wet string, which showed that lightning is electricity.
In 1753 the Royal Society gave Franklin its gold medal, and Harvard and Yale gave him honorary degrees. He took no money from his inventions, because he wanted everyone to share their benefits.
In 1749 Franklin wrote a plan for a new school, and he gave copies free to the leading citizens. When they had read it, he asked them to pledge money, to be paid over five years.
The Academy opened in 1751 in a large hall that had once been built for Whitefield's sermons. In time it grew into the University of Pennsylvania.
Dr Thomas Bond wanted to open a hospital for the sick poor, but few people were willing to pay for it. People kept asking whether Franklin had been consulted, so Bond came to him for help.
Franklin asked Bond to explain his plan, and he thought it was a good one. Before asking for money, he wrote about it in the newspaper so that people could think about it first.
The Assembly would not pay for a hospital in the city, so Franklin offered a bill that promised two thousand pounds. The money would be given only after private citizens raised the same amount.
Gifts soon passed the amount needed, and the Assembly paid its promised money. A handsome hospital was built, and Franklin wrote the words on its cornerstone.
In 1751, the people of Philadelphia elected Franklin to the Assembly, and they kept choosing him for years. In 1753 he also became joint postmaster-general for all the colonies.
In 1754, war with France was coming, so representatives of the colonies were called to meet at Albany. On the way, Franklin wrote a plan to unite them all under one government.
In May 1754, Franklin printed a picture of a snake cut into pieces in his newspaper. Each piece stood for a colony, and the words below said Join, or Die.
At Albany, the delegates debated Franklin's plan for many days. At last they agreed to it, and they sent copies to the Board of Trade and to the colonial assemblies.
The colonial assemblies thought Franklin's plan gave the Crown too much power. In England it was thought to give the people too much, and so both sides rejected it.

Governor Morris and the Assembly quarrelled about taxes, because the Proprietors would not pay tax on their own land. Franklin wrote many of the Assembly's replies, yet the lively governor still invited him to dinner.
In 1755, General Braddock came from England with two regiments to attack a French fort. He was angry with Pennsylvania's Assembly, so the Assembly sent Franklin to speak with him.
Braddock told Franklin that he did not have enough wagons for the army. Franklin said that almost every farmer in Pennsylvania had one, and he agreed to find them.

At Lancaster, Franklin posted a notice asking farmers to hire out their wagons and horses at good daily rates. He warned that if they refused, an officer would come with soldiers and take them by force.
The farmers trusted Franklin, and he promised to pay them with his own bond. Within two weeks, 150 wagons and 259 pack horses set off to join the army.
Franklin heard that the army's young officers were poor, so he arranged a gift for them. Twenty parcels of tea, sugar, coffee, cheese, ham and wine were sent, each loaded on a horse.
Franklin warned Braddock that his army's long thin line could be attacked by surprise from the forest. Braddock smiled and said that trained British soldiers could not be beaten that way.
On 9 July 1755, French and Native forces ambushed Braddock's army in the forest. Braddock was badly wounded and died a few days later.
After the defeat, the farmers whose wagons and horses were lost came to Franklin for payment. He had signed a bond for large sums, and he was in danger of being ruined.
After the defeat, Franklin wrote a bill for a voluntary militia, which left the Quakers free to stay out. To win support, he also printed a dialogue that answered every objection he could think of.
In late 1755, attacks on frontier settlements killed many people, and a Moravian mission was destroyed. The governor asked Franklin to organise the defence, and although he was no soldier, he agreed.
Franklin marched to Bethlehem, the main Moravian town, and was surprised to find it well defended. The town had a stockade, guns, and even paving stones piled at the windows.
Franklin's men cut down pine trees and built a wooden fort in about a week, even though it rained hard every other day. They placed a small swivel gun at one corner and fired it to warn enemies.

Franklin noticed that men are happiest when they have work to do. The chaplain, Mr Beatty, complained that few men came to prayers, so Franklin suggested that he give out the daily rum just after them.
In early 1756, Franklin handed the command to an experienced officer and returned to Philadelphia. The militia there had elected him colonel, and its officers rode out with drawn swords to meet him.

In August 1756, the new governor, Denny, gave Franklin the gold medal of the Royal Society at a public dinner. In private he hinted that the Proprietors would reward Franklin if he stopped opposing them.
The quarrel over taxing the Proprietors' land never ended. In 1757 the Assembly chose Franklin to carry its complaints to the king in London, and he agreed.
Franklin travelled to New York to sail on the mail ship, but the commander, Lord Loudoun, was slow to finish his letters. Each day Loudoun said the ship would sail soon, and each day it did not.

In the waiting room, Franklin met a messenger named Innis, who had waited weeks for his own letters. Innis said that Loudoun was like St George on the inn signs, always on his horse and never riding on.
At last, in June 1757, Franklin sailed from New York for England. After a fast voyage, the ship came dangerously close to rocks in the dark, but it escaped and landed safely in July.
Franklin wrote his book in several parts, and the story stops in 1757. He lived until 1790, when he died at the age of eighty-four.
C1C2: In the summer of 1771, Benjamin Franklin was a guest at a peaceful country house in England, far from the noise and quarrels of London. He took up his pen and began a long letter to his son William, who was then the governor of New Jersey. The letter would grow into one of the most famous life stories ever written, although its author never finished it.

Franklin confessed that he was an old man, and that old men love to tell stories about the past. He hoped that his family might enjoy reading how he had risen from a humble start, and what lessons that journey had taught him. If he were offered the chance to live his life again, he wrote, he would accept at once, asking only that he might correct its errors as a printer corrects the mistakes of a first edition.

Ecton was a small village in Northamptonshire, and the Franklins had farmed a little land there for about three hundred years, perhaps longer. The word franklin had once meant a free landowner, which is how the family came by its name, and in each generation the eldest son was trained to be the village blacksmith. Franklin visited the place himself in 1758 and walked among the old houses, searching for any trace of the family that had come before him.

Franklin learned many of these family stories from his uncle Thomas, a blacksmith who was also the cleverest and most public-spirited man in the village. Thomas helped his neighbours, wrote their documents for them and took a lively interest in the affairs of the whole district, and people remembered him with respect. He died four years to the day before Benjamin was born, a coincidence that Franklin noted with quiet amusement.

In the reign of Queen Mary, when it was dangerous to own an English Bible, Franklin's great-great-grandfather kept one fastened open with tapes beneath a joint stool. When he wished to read to his family, he turned the stool upside down on his knees, while a child stood by the door to watch for an officer of the church court. At the first warning the stool was turned back on its feet, and the hidden Bible was safe.

Franklin's uncle Benjamin had worked as a silk dyer in London, but in his old age he crossed the ocean and lived for years in his brother's house in Boston. He loved verse and wrote a great many poems, and he filled volumes with sermons in a shorthand of his own invention. Young Benjamin, who was named after him, became a favourite of the old man, who even offered to leave him those books.

Josiah Franklin worshipped in a way that the law of England forbade, and the meetings of his small church were often disturbed. Some of his friends decided to leave for New England, where they hoped to practise their religion in freedom, and about 1682 Josiah sailed with them, taking his wife and three children. He had been trained as a dyer, but in Boston that trade could not support a growing family, so he turned to making candles and soap.

Josiah was a strong man with a sound mind and a pair of unusually clever hands, and he could draw a little and play the violin. In the evening he would sing hymns in a clear voice while the family listened, and the sound carried pleasantly through the house. People who were worried about their business or the affairs of the town often came to him for advice, for his judgement was widely respected.

Abiah Folger, Josiah's second wife, was the daughter of Peter Folger, one of the first settlers of the island of Nantucket. Franklin remembered her as a discreet and sensible woman who nursed all ten of her own children herself. Together with the seven children of Josiah's first marriage, they made a household so large that seventeen children passed through it.

In January 1706 Benjamin was born in Boston, the youngest of Josiah's sons and the youngest child but two in that crowded house. He later remembered seeing thirteen of them seated together at his father's table, and all had grown up to be men and women. The household was a busy and noisy one, and it was there that the boy first learned how hard a family must work to earn its bread.

Josiah had decided to give his youngest son to the service of the Church, as the family's gift of one tenth of its sons. Benjamin learned to read so early that, in later life, he could not remember a time when he had not been able to do it. His father and his friends praised the boy's quick mind, and they all agreed that he would make an excellent minister.

At eight years old Benjamin was sent to the grammar school in Boston, where he rose to the top of his class and was promised a double promotion. Yet within a year his father changed his mind, partly because the cost of a long education was heavy for such a large family. He also remarked that many learned men of the town lived poor lives, and he decided that a different path might serve his son better.

Josiah next sent his son to a school kept by a Mr Brownell, who was gentle and encouraging and taught writing and arithmetic. Under his care Benjamin soon learned to write a good hand, but he made no progress in arithmetic and was ashamed of it. At ten years old his schooling came to an end altogether, and he went to work in his father's shop.

In his father's shop Benjamin cut wicks for the candles, poured melted tallow into the moulds, minded the counter and ran errands through the streets of Boston. He soon grew to hate the greasy, smelly trade, and he felt a strong desire to go to sea. He gave no sign of how much he disliked the work, but his father could see that the boy's mind was far away from the shop.

From his earliest childhood Benjamin was fond of the water, and he swam like a fish long before most boys could manage a few strokes. He also learned to handle boats and canoes, and when he was out with other boys in a boat he was usually trusted to steer. In every game or adventure he was generally the leader, though he admitted that he sometimes led his friends into trouble.

Beside a mill pond in Boston there was a marsh where the boys stood to catch small fish, and the mud was soon trampled into a mess. Benjamin proposed that they build a wharf, and one evening the whole gang carried off a heap of stones that had been set aside for a new house. The workmen discovered the theft the next morning, several of the boys were punished, and although Benjamin argued that the wharf was useful, his father told him that nothing is truly useful which is not also honest.

Josiah feared that his restless son might run away to sea, so he walked him around Boston to watch joiners, bricklayers, turners and brass workers at their work. Benjamin enjoyed seeing skilled hands make useful things, and he learned a good deal about handling tools. It was a lesson that would serve him well in later life, when he made small machines for his own experiments.

Josiah wanted his son to learn the cutler's trade, and for a few days Benjamin was sent on trial to his cousin Samuel, who had learned that craft in London. Samuel, however, demanded a fee for teaching him which Josiah considered much too high. The boy was therefore taken home again, to his great disappointment, and he went back to the candles and the soap.

Josiah always invited a sensible friend or neighbour to dine, and he steered the conversation toward subjects that were useful, wise or just. The children were encouraged to listen, and their minds were turned away from the dishes in front of them. Benjamin later said that he was so little aware of what he ate that he could hardly remember a single dinner of his childhood.

From the time he was a small boy Benjamin spent every penny that came into his hands on books, and he read whatever he could borrow or buy. The shop was dull and the days were long, but a book could carry him anywhere in the world. By the time he was twelve, reading had become the greatest pleasure of his life, and he was determined that no trade should take it away from him.

Josiah owned a small library, and most of its volumes were long and heavy arguments about points of religion. Benjamin read a good many of them, because he was hungry for anything printed, though he later felt that this was not the best use of his time. Among the dull volumes, however, he found a few real treasures, and one of them was an odd volume of Plutarch's Lives, which he read over and over.

Benjamin's first great love was the work of John Bunyan, whose Pilgrim's Progress he read so often that the pages grew soft. Later he sold all of Bunyan's works in order to buy Burton's Historical Collections, a set of forty or fifty little cheap volumes of history and travel. Chapmen sold those books from door to door, and the boy found them a very good bargain for his small supply of pennies.

Two other books made a deep impression on the growing boy, Daniel Defoe's Essay on Projects and Cotton Mather's Essays to Do Good. Both were full of plans for helping one's neighbours and improving the life of a town. Franklin believed that these books gave him a turn of mind that guided many of the most important actions of his later life.

Benjamin's older brother James had learned the printing trade in London, and in 1717 he returned to Boston with a press and a fine set of type. The boy's love of books made printing seem the natural trade for him, and his father soon agreed. Josiah worried that Benjamin, who still longed for the sea, might run away like another of his sons, and he wanted to settle the matter quickly.

At twelve years old Benjamin, still hesitating, was persuaded to sign a contract that bound him as an apprentice to his brother until he was twenty-one. It was a very long time for a boy to serve, and only in the final year would he be paid the wages of a skilled worker. Yet he took to the trade quickly, and before long he had become a useful help to James in the shop.

As an apprentice Benjamin made rapid progress, and soon he was far more useful to his brother than he had been at the beginning. He gained access to better books through the booksellers' boys, and a kind customer named Matthew Adams, who owned a fine library, invited him to borrow whatever he liked. Benjamin often sat up most of the night to read a volume, returning it clean and early in the morning so that its owner would never miss it.

At this time Benjamin tried his hand at poetry, and he wrote two ballads which his brother encouraged him to print and sell in the streets. One, called The Lighthouse Tragedy, told of a sea captain and his two daughters who were drowned, and the other was a sailor's song about the capture of the pirate Blackbeard. They were poor stuff, written in the style of street ballads, but they sold very well, and the success flattered the young author's pride.

When Josiah saw the ballads, he laughed at them and warned his son that makers of verses were generally beggars. Benjamin took the warning to heart, and he escaped the fate of becoming a very bad poet. Instead he gave his energy to prose, which he came to see as the surest road to being useful to others and perhaps to being rewarded too.

Benjamin and his friend John Collins began to argue by letter over whether women should be given a learned education, and Benjamin took the opposite side simply for the pleasure of the debate. One day Josiah found the letters, read them closely and, without taking either side, pointed out that Benjamin's spelling and punctuation were good but that he fell far short of Collins in elegance of expression, in method and in clarity. Benjamin saw that his father was right, and from that day he resolved to improve his writing by every means he could find.

At about this time Benjamin came across an odd volume of The Spectator, a collection of elegant essays that had appeared in the London magazine of that name. He had never seen the work before, and he bought it and read it over and over again with delight. The writing seemed to him excellent, and he longed with all his heart to be able to imitate it.

To learn the style of The Spectator, Benjamin took short notes on the meaning of each sentence and put them aside for several days. He then tried to write the whole essay again in his own words, using as fine a language as he could find, and compared his version to the original. He soon discovered many faults, and he saw that he lacked a stock of words, which he might have had if he had kept up the habit of writing verse.

Because verse demands many different words that rhyme and fit a rhythm, Benjamin sometimes turned the tales of The Spectator into poems, and some days later changed them back into prose. He also jumbled his notes at random, set them aside for weeks, and then tried to arrange them in the best order before comparing them with the original essay. Occasionally he found that his own arrangement was better than that of the great author, which encouraged him to think that he might one day be an acceptable writer.

At sixteen Benjamin, who had once failed arithmetic at school, took up Cocker's book on the subject and worked through every page by himself with surprising ease. He then read two books on navigation by Seller and Sturmy, and from them he gained a little knowledge of geometry, although he never advanced far in that science. The experience taught him that a subject which seems impossible in a classroom may become easy when a person studies it alone, at his own pace.

Benjamin also read John Locke's famous Essay Concerning Human Understanding and a French book on logic known as The Art of Thinking. Between them these authors showed him how to reason carefully, to define his terms and to follow an argument step by step. He found that disciplined thought could be as pleasant as any game, and he began to enjoy the company of ideas.

In a book about the Greek thinker Socrates, Benjamin read of a method that taught him to ask humble questions and let the other person find the flaws in his own case. Delighted by the idea, he gave up bluntly contradicting people and took to modest enquiries that led his companions, step by step, into admitting a mistake. He used the habit with great pleasure for years, though in time he kept only the modest manner and dropped the tricks of questioning.

Benjamin gradually stopped using words that gave an air of certainty, such as undoubtedly or certainly, and he preferred to say I think, I imagine or it seems to me. He found that the people around him listened more kindly, resisted him less and gave way more easily when he was wrong. A line of the poet Pope, advising that men should be taught as if they were not taught at all, confirmed him in the habit.

At sixteen Benjamin came across a book by Thomas Tryon that recommended a diet made of vegetables alone, and he resolved to try it. His brother, who boarded the apprentices with another family, found it inconvenient to cook special meals for him, and the household complained about his fussy habits. Benjamin, meanwhile, had begun to enjoy the experiment, and he learned to prepare a few dishes of rice, potatoes and hasty pudding for himself.

Benjamin told his brother that if he were given half of the money that was paid for his board, he would feed himself. James agreed at once, and Benjamin found that he could save half of that sum again, which he spent on books. While the others went out to dinner he ate a biscuit or a handful of raisins with a glass of water, and he used the rest of the hour to study, finding that his mind grew clearer and quicker.

Years afterward, on a voyage, the crew caught some cod and fried them, and Benjamin found the smell almost impossible to resist. He had always believed that killing fish was a kind of murder, but when he saw smaller fish inside the cod he decided that, if they ate one another, he might fairly eat them too. He dined on cod with a hearty appetite, and he remarked that it is very convenient to be a reasonable creature, since reason can always supply an excuse for whatever one wishes to do.

In 1721 James Franklin began to print a newspaper called the New-England Courant, the second to appear in America. Some of his friends thought that one newspaper was plenty for the colonies and that it could not succeed, but James went ahead anyway. Benjamin set the type, worked the press and carried the printed papers through the streets of Boston to customers, with great enjoyment of his own part in the venture.

Benjamin longed to see his own writing in the paper, but he was sure that his brother would never print the work of a mere apprentice. He therefore disguised his handwriting, composed an essay, and slipped it under the door of the printing house late at night. In the morning, the pages were found, and James read them to his friends who came to the shop.

James's friends took the pages from his hand, read them aloud in the shop and praised the writing warmly. They tried to guess the author, and, to Benjamin's secret delight, they named only the cleverest and most learned men in the colony. He was proud to have such judges, though he suspected that they were not as wise as they looked.

Benjamin invented a character called Silence Dogood, a countrywoman and a minister's widow, who had opinions on everything. In fourteen letters that appeared in the Courant, she poked fun at the follies of the town, such as foolish fashions, drunkenness and the bad habits of the students at Harvard. The readers loved her wit, and many of them wondered who she could be.

Eventually, when the praise had grown loud, Benjamin confessed to James that he was the author of the letters. The older brother was not nearly as pleased as the boy had expected, because he thought that praise would make his apprentice vain, and perhaps he felt a touch of jealousy as well. This was probably one reason why the two brothers began to quarrel more often, and the bad feeling grew.

As an apprentice, Benjamin was bound to obey his brother, and James sometimes beat him when he thought the boy was being saucy or slow. Benjamin believed that this harsh and unfair treatment gave him a lasting dislike of arbitrary power, a feeling that stayed with him all his life. He admitted, however, that he was a provoking boy, and that he had a share in the blame.

In 1722 the Courant printed an article that criticised the government, and the Assembly ordered James to be put in jail for a month. Benjamin was also taken before the council and questioned, but he would not tell them who had written the piece, and they let him go, perhaps thinking that an apprentice was bound to keep his master's secrets. While James was locked up, Benjamin ran the paper alone and enjoyed writing sharp little pieces against the people in power.

Early in 1723 the Assembly ordered that James Franklin should no longer print the Courant, and the problem was how to keep the paper alive. His friends proposed that it should be published under the name of Benjamin Franklin, and to avoid any complaint that a master was using his apprentice, James returned the boy's original agreement. Privately, however, Benjamin was made to sign a new set of papers that bound him again, a trick so thin that it could not have stood up in any court.

The old quarrels soon returned, and one day James struck his brother in anger. Benjamin knew that his brother would never dare to produce the secret agreement, since that would reveal the trick, and so he declared himself free and left the print shop. Years later he admitted that this was not entirely a fair thing to do, and he counted it among the mistakes of his youth.

James went to every printer in Boston and asked them not to employ his brother, so Benjamin could find no work in the town. His father took James's side in the quarrel, which hurt the boy deeply, and Benjamin decided that he would leave Boston altogether. His friend John Collins helped him to arrange a place on a sloop bound for New York, and Benjamin sold some of his books to raise a little money for the journey.

To explain why he had to leave without telling his family, Benjamin gave the captain a story that made him a young man in trouble, and the sloop slipped out of Boston harbour at dawn. In only three days he reached New York at the age of seventeen, three hundred miles from home, with very little money and not one friend or recommendation in the whole town. Yet he was young, healthy and sure of himself, and he did not mean to turn back.

In New York Benjamin went straight to William Bradford, the old printer who had helped to start printing in Pennsylvania, but Bradford had no work to give him. He explained that his son Andrew, a printer in Philadelphia, had lately lost his chief assistant, and that the young man might find a place there. Philadelphia was a hundred miles away, and Benjamin, who had very little money, set out at once.

A fierce squall struck the little boat as it crossed the bay, tearing the sail and throwing the passengers into a panic. A drunken Dutchman was thrown into the water, and Benjamin, leaning out, caught him by the hair and hauled him back on board. Wet and shivering, the man asked Benjamin to dry a book from his pocket, and it proved to be Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress in Dutch, printed far more handsomely than it had ever been in English.

The wind drove the boat toward Long Island, where the surf was so heavy that no one could land, and the passengers were forced to anchor for the night. They were cold, wet and hungry, and for nearly thirty hours they had little to eat or drink except a small bottle of rum and some dirty water from the bay. When Benjamin finally reached the shore he had a fever, so he remembered something he had read about drinking cold water, and by sweating through the night he cured himself.

From Amboy Benjamin set out on foot for Burlington, about fifty miles away, and the rain fell steadily all day until he was wet to the skin. Late in the evening he stopped at a small inn, where his dirty clothes and his awkward answers to questions made the people suspect that he was a runaway servant. A travelling doctor named Brown, who loved books and jokes, took a liking to him, and the two struck up a friendship that lasted as long as the doctor lived.

At Burlington Benjamin found that the regular boat had just left, and he had little money to spend on an inn. An old woman who sold gingerbread took pity on him, cooked him a hot dinner and let him rest at her house until another boat should pass. When one came by at last, there was no wind, so the passengers took the oars and rowed through the dark hours, and about midnight they landed, lit a fire with fence rails and waited for daylight.

On a Sunday morning in October Benjamin stepped ashore at the Market Street wharf in Philadelphia, dirty from his journey, with his pockets stuffed with shirts and stockings. He had only a silver dollar and a shilling in copper coins, and the copper went to the boatmen, who had at first refused it because he had helped to row. He then asked at a baker's for bread, and was handed three large puffy rolls for his money.

Benjamin walked up Market Street with a roll under each arm and another in his mouth, feeling hungry and rather pleased with his bargain. At her father's door a young woman named Deborah Read saw him pass and thought, as he admitted himself, that he made a most awkward and ridiculous appearance. After a circuit of several streets he came back to the river for a drink of water, and, since one roll was enough, he gave the other two to a woman and child from the boat.

Feeling tired, Benjamin followed a group of quiet, well-dressed people along the street and found himself in the great meeting house of the Quakers. He sat among them, waiting for someone to speak, but nobody said a word, and since he had not slept the night before he soon fell fast asleep. He slept until the meeting broke up, when someone kindly woke him, and so the first house he entered in Philadelphia was a house of prayer.

Benjamin made his way to Andrew Bradford, the printer to whom he had been sent, and was given breakfast and a kind welcome. Bradford had no work to offer, since he already had a helper, but he said that a new printer called Keimer might need one. His father, William Bradford, who had arrived on horseback ahead of the boat, offered to go with Benjamin and introduce him to Keimer.

Samuel Keimer's print shop was a poor place, with a crazy old press and a single small set of worn type, which he was using to compose a poem of mourning for his friend Aquila Rose. He wrote it straight into the type from his head, without any copy on paper, so that no one could help him with the work. Benjamin put the press in order, printed the poem when it was ready, and was soon given regular work and a room in the house of Mr Read, whose daughter Deborah had laughed at him.

Benjamin soon made friends among the young men of Philadelphia who loved to read, and three of them became his close companions: Charles Osborne, Joseph Watson and James Ralph. Watson was a devout and honest man, Osborne was sensible but severe in his judgements, and Ralph was a charming talker who wrote poetry. On Sundays the four of them walked in the woods beside the Schuylkill River and read aloud to one another, and Franklin remembered those afternoons with great pleasure.

Keimer was a strange man with strange beliefs, for he wore a long beard because an old law said that it should not be trimmed, and he kept Saturday as his day of rest. He loved to argue about religion, and Benjamin, using the questioning method he had learned from Socrates, often left him puzzled and confused. Keimer grew so fond of these debates that he proposed to found a new sect with Benjamin as its chief preacher, and Benjamin, who did not take it seriously, agreed on one condition.

Benjamin said that he would accept the Saturday rest if Keimer would give up eating meat, and Keimer, who dearly loved his food, agreed to try it. For three months the two of them lived on vegetables and puddings, which suited Benjamin very well, but Keimer grew weary of the diet and finally ordered a roast pig for a dinner with friends. When the pig arrived early he could not resist the smell, and he ate the whole animal himself before the guests came.

Benjamin's brother-in-law, Captain Holmes, showed the governor of Pennsylvania a letter that Benjamin had written, and Sir William Keith was astonished that its author was so young. One day Benjamin and Keimer saw the governor and a Colonel French crossing the street in fine clothes, and Keimer ran downstairs, thinking that the visit was meant for him. It was Benjamin that the governor wanted, however, and he praised the young man with a politeness that Benjamin had never experienced, and carried him off to a tavern to taste some excellent Madeira wine.

Over their wine the governor told Benjamin that the printers of Philadelphia were wretched and that he would certainly succeed if he set up for himself. Keith promised to secure him the public printing and to do him every other service in his power, and he offered to write to Josiah to explain the plan and ask for his support. Benjamin accepted gratefully, kept the matter from Keimer, and in April 1724 took a boat for Boston with the governor's letter in his pocket.

After seven months away, Benjamin surprised his family by walking into Boston in a handsome new suit, with a watch in his pocket and nearly five pounds in silver. Everyone welcomed him warmly except James, who looked him over coldly at the print shop and returned to his work. When the workers asked about Philadelphia, Benjamin spread his silver on the bench, showed them his watch, and gave them a coin to drink his health, an offence that James never forgave.

Josiah read the governor's letter with surprise, and when Captain Holmes returned he remarked that a man who would set up an eighteen-year-old in business must have very little judgement. He refused to lend the money, but he wrote kindly to Benjamin, urging him to behave respectfully and to avoid insulting others in print, a fault to which he thought his son was inclined. If Benjamin saved carefully until he was twenty-one, his father promised, he would help him find the rest of the money, and with that hope and his parents' blessing Benjamin prepared to sail back.

On his return journey Benjamin stopped at Newport to visit his brother John, who had moved there and who welcomed him with warm affection. John's friend, a Mr Vernon, was owed about thirty-five pounds in Pennsylvania, and he asked Benjamin to collect it and to hold it until he received instructions on how to send it. This favour, which seemed small and friendly, was later to cause the young man a great deal of anxiety.

When Benjamin reached New York, the captain of the sloop mentioned to Governor Burnet that one of his passengers owned a great many books, and the governor asked to meet him. He showed Benjamin his own large library, and the two spent a pleasant hour discussing books and authors. Benjamin was delighted that a second governor should notice a poor boy like himself, and the visit gave him a good deal of confidence.

In New York Collins took to drinking brandy and gambling, and soon he had lost his own money and borrowed Benjamin's, including some of the money that belonged to Mr Vernon. On the river near Philadelphia he was too drunk to row and threatened to throw Benjamin overboard, so Benjamin, knowing that his friend swam well, tipped him into the water instead. They hardly spoke afterwards, and Collins went off to the West Indies without paying his debts, leaving Benjamin uneasy until the day he could repay Vernon himself.

Back in Philadelphia, Benjamin told the governor that his father had refused to help, and Keith answered that he would pay for the business himself. He proposed to send the young man to London to choose a printing press and type, and he promised to supply letters of credit that would let Benjamin buy what he needed on the governor's word. Meanwhile Benjamin returned to work for Keimer, and he and Deborah Read, who had grown fond of each other, agreed with her mother that any marriage must wait until his return.

In November 1724 Benjamin sailed for London with his friend James Ralph, who had left his wife and child behind in Philadelphia, and with a Quaker merchant named Denham among their fellow passengers. The governor had promised that his letters of credit would be waiting in the ship's bag of mail, and the captain agreed to let Benjamin search it once they reached the English Channel. When the bag was opened, however, Benjamin searched it carefully and found no letter that would give him a penny of credit.

In London a friendly merchant, Mr Denham, laughed at the idea that the governor could have sent any letters of credit, for Keith had no credit himself and no sensible person relied on him. Benjamin came to see that Keith was not a cruel man but a weak one, who wished to oblige everybody and, having little else to give, gave people hopes. Left alone in a huge city with no money for a press, he and Ralph took a cheap room in Little Britain at three shillings and sixpence a week, and began to look for work.

James Ralph had no wish to return to America, and he dreamed of becoming an actor or a poet instead of looking for ordinary work. Benjamin, who had found a job in a printing house, supported his friend for months, lending him about twenty-seven pounds that he never saw again. Ralph read his long poems aloud for advice, and Benjamin honestly told him that he would never be an excellent poet, a judgement that Ralph did not enjoy.

At Palmer's, a famous printing house in Bartholomew Close, Benjamin worked diligently for nearly a year, although he spent too much of his earnings on plays with Ralph. While setting the type for Wollaston's The Religion of Nature, he found some of the arguments weak, and he wrote a little pamphlet of his own, called A Dissertation on Liberty and Necessity, Pleasure and Pain. Palmer thought its doctrines shocking, and Franklin later counted the pamphlet among the mistakes of his youth.

In London the pamphlet brought Benjamin to the notice of a surgeon named Lyons, who introduced him to Dr Mandeville, the witty author of The Fable of the Bees. Mandeville led a club at a tavern in Cheapside, and Dr Pemberton, whom Benjamin met through the same friend, promised to introduce him to Sir Isaac Newton, though he never did. Sir Hans Sloane, meanwhile, bought a purse of asbestos that Benjamin had brought from America, and invited him to his house to see his famous collection of curiosities.

While he was busy with work, plays and new friends, Benjamin let his feelings for Deborah Read fade, and in all his months in London he wrote to her only once. His letter told her that he was not likely to return soon, and it must have hurt her deeply, since she was waiting for him at home. Franklin later called this one of the great mistakes of his life, and wrote that it was a fault he would most wish to correct if he could live again.

Benjamin moved to Watts's, a large printing house near Lincoln's Inn Fields that employed about fifty men, and at first he worked at the press for the sake of the exercise. The other workers drank beer all day long, but Benjamin drank only water, and he carried a heavy form of type in each hand up and down the stairs while the others carried one in both. He told them that a penny loaf held more flour than a pint of beer held grain, and a few were convinced, giving up their beer for a breakfast of hot gruel with pepper and bread.

When Benjamin moved to the composing room, the men demanded five shillings from him as a welcome payment, which he refused because he had already paid it in the press room. The master supported him, but for two or three weeks he was treated like an outcast, and little pieces of mischief spoiled his work, which the workers blamed on the ghost of the chapel. In the end Benjamin paid, having learned that it is foolish to be on bad terms with the people one must live with every day.

Benjamin had always been a strong swimmer, and one day with a friend he swam all the way down the Thames from Chelsea to Blackfriars, performing many feats of skill both on the water and beneath it. The tricks surprised and delighted the people who watched from boats and from the bank. Word reached a nobleman, Sir William Wyndham, who asked him to teach his two sons to swim, and for a while Benjamin thought seriously of opening a swimming school in England.

After eighteen months in London, Benjamin grew tired of the city and remembered the happy months he had spent in Pennsylvania, so he was glad when Mr Denham offered to take him back as his clerk. Denham promised to teach him to keep accounts, to copy letters and to tend the store, and later to send him to the West Indies with a cargo of flour and bread. The wage of fifty pounds a year was less than Benjamin earned as a printer, but the prospect was better, and he agreed at once.

In July 1726 the ship Berkshire sailed from Gravesend, and Benjamin kept a detailed journal of the long voyage across the Atlantic. The most important part of that journal, he later said, was a plan that he made at sea for regulating his conduct in life. It was remarkable that a man of twenty should form such a plan, and more remarkable still that he kept to it fairly faithfully all the way to old age.

Benjamin landed at Philadelphia on 11 October 1726 and found that a great deal had changed while he was away. Sir William Keith was no longer governor, and when Benjamin met him walking in the street, the old man seemed ashamed and passed without a word. Deborah Read, whose friends had despaired of his return, had married a potter named Rogers, but she was never happy with him and soon parted from him.

Denham and Benjamin opened their store in Water Street, and they lodged and took their meals together, so that the merchant could teach his clerk the secrets of trade. Denham gave advice as a father would, because he had a sincere regard for the young man, and Benjamin respected and loved him in return. If nothing had gone wrong, the two might have lived and worked together happily for many years, and Benjamin might have become a merchant.

Early in 1727, soon after Benjamin's twenty-first birthday, both he and Mr Denham fell ill, and Benjamin's illness was a pleurisy that very nearly killed him. He suffered a good deal and had made up his mind to die, and he was almost disappointed to find himself recovering, because it meant that he would have to go through the same hard business again some day. His friend was less fortunate, for Denham lingered for a long time and then died, leaving Benjamin a small sum in his will as a token of his kindness.

After Denham's death Benjamin went back to Keimer, who now had a larger shop, plenty of new type and a crowd of workers, none of whom was any good at the trade. Keimer offered him a large wage to manage the printing house, and Benjamin guessed that Keimer meant to dismiss him as soon as the workers, including the honest Welshman Hugh Meredith, had learned enough. Benjamin accepted anyway, since he needed the money, and he taught the whole crowd, among them the witty Stephen Potts and the Oxford scholar George Webb.

Keimer's shop was always short of supplies, and since there was no foundry in America to cast type, Benjamin set out to make it himself. He had once watched letters being cast in London, so he built a mould, used the letters they already owned as punches and struck new moulds from them in lead. He also engraved ornaments, mixed the ink and kept the warehouse, until he was, in his own words, quite a factotum.

One day Keimer saw Benjamin looking out of a window at a noise in the street, and he shouted at him to mind his business, in a loud and angry voice that all the neighbours could hear. Benjamin was nettled by the public insult, and when Keimer followed him inside and gave him a quarter's notice, he declared that he would leave that very minute, took his hat and walked out of the door. Hugh Meredith, whose father had some money, soon offered to set up a printing house with him, and they sent to London for a press and type.

Keimer won the contract to print the paper money of New Jersey, and since only Benjamin could cut the ornaments and supply the right types, he sent a very civil message asking him to return. Benjamin devised a copperplate press, the first ever seen in the country, and at Burlington a committee of leading citizens came by turns to watch the printing and found his conversation more interesting than his master's. The gentlemen invited him to their homes and introduced him to their friends, while Keimer was a little neglected.

When the press and type arrived from London, Benjamin and Hugh Meredith rented a house near the market and opened their own printing house. A friend named George House brought them a countryman who wanted a printer, and the five shillings that this man paid were their first earnings, which came at a moment when all their cash was spent. Franklin wrote that this small sum gave him more pleasure than any crown he earned afterwards, and the gratitude he felt for House made him ready ever after to help young people who were starting out.

In the autumn of 1727 Benjamin formed most of his clever acquaintances into a club for mutual improvement, which he called the Junto. The members were mostly young tradesmen, which is why it was sometimes known as the Leather Apron Club, and they met every Friday evening in a tavern to discuss questions of morals, politics and natural science. Each member took turns to raise a question, and the rules were designed to keep the conversation pleasant rather than quarrelsome.

Among the first members were Joseph Breintnall, a kindly copyist who loved poetry, and Thomas Godfrey, a self-taught mathematician who worked as a glazier. There were also Nicholas Scull the surveyor, William Parsons the shoemaker, who studied mathematics for fun, and William Maugridge, a sensible joiner. Franklin also counted Hugh Meredith, Stephen Potts, George Webb, the generous young gentleman Robert Grace, and William Coleman, who had the clearest head and the best heart of all.

Each member in turn had to produce questions on morals, politics or natural science for the others to discuss, and every three months he had to read an essay of his own. The debates were to be conducted in a sincere spirit of inquiry, without any love of dispute or desire for victory. To keep tempers cool, expressions of certainty and direct contradiction were soon forbidden, and anyone who used them paid a small fine.

The Junto went on for many years, and Franklin thought it the best school of philosophy, morals and politics that then existed in the province. The questions were read a week before each meeting, so that members could think about them, and the habit made the club a place where friendships and plans were born. Members also helped one another in business, and Breintnall, for example, won for Franklin and Meredith the printing of forty sheets of a history of the Quakers.

Franklin had formed a plan to publish a newspaper, and he confided it to only one man, George Webb, who promptly told Keimer. Keimer, wishing to defeat him, at once announced that he would print a paper himself, with Webb as his helper. Franklin was angry at the betrayal, but his own press was not yet ready, so for the moment he could do nothing but wait.

While waiting, Franklin wrote a series of amusing essays called the Busy-Body for Andrew Bradford's newspaper, and Breintnall continued them for several months, so that the public paid little attention to Keimer's plans. Keimer started his paper anyway, but after about three-quarters of a year he had no more than ninety subscribers and he offered it to Franklin for a trifle. Franklin, who had been ready for some time, took it over at once, dropped its long name and called it the Pennsylvania Gazette, and within a few years it proved extremely profitable.

Franklin soon made the Gazette a far better paper than it had been in Keimer's hands, with clear printing and lively writing. His spirited remarks on the quarrel between Governor Burnet and the Massachusetts Assembly impressed the principal men of the province, and the newspaper and its editor were widely talked about. Within a few weeks most of them had become subscribers, and others followed their example.

In 1729 the people of Pennsylvania cried out for more paper money, but wealthy men opposed it, fearing that it would lose its value and injure those who had lent money. Franklin, who thought that the earlier issue had done great good for trade and employment, wrote an anonymous pamphlet in its favour, and the common people welcomed it. The rich could find no writer to answer him, the Assembly voted for the money, and his friends there rewarded him with the profitable work of printing it.

Hugh Meredith was often drunk in the streets, and his father could not pay his share of what they owed for the press, so the partners were sued. Two true friends, William Coleman and Robert Grace, came to Franklin separately, without any request from him, and each offered to lend him whatever he needed to take over the whole business. Meredith agreed to leave for North Carolina, where he wanted to farm, and Franklin, who never forgot the kindness of his two friends, took on all the debts and carried on alone.

One night a form of type, already set for the next day's printing, broke apart by accident, and Franklin patiently set the whole of it again before he went to bed. His neighbours noticed such habits, and at a club of merchants Dr Baird declared that he never passed the new printing house without seeing Franklin at work, late at night or before others were out of bed. Soon a merchant offered him supplies of stationery, and Franklin, to show he was not above any task, sometimes wheeled home his paper through the streets on a barrow.

Deborah Read's husband, Rogers, had run away to the West Indies, and it was rumoured that he had another wife and had died there. Nobody could prove either story, and a legal difficulty hung over any new marriage, but Franklin and Deborah had revived their old affection for each other. They decided to take the risk, and they were married on 1 September 1730, with no ill consequences, as Franklin happily recorded.

Deborah proved to be a good and faithful partner, and she helped her husband greatly by attending the shop, folding and stitching pamphlets, and buying old linen rags for the paper makers. The two lived plainly and worked side by side, and Franklin wrote that they prospered together and that each had always tried to make the other happy. Their son William, who was born about this time, grew up in the household, and Deborah helped to raise him.

For breakfast Franklin ate bread and milk from a cheap earthen bowl with a pewter spoon, and he thought it quite enough. One morning he found the milk in a china bowl with a silver spoon beside it, which his wife had bought for twenty-three shillings because she thought her husband deserved them as much as any neighbour. That was how luxury first entered his house, and over the years the silver and china grew to be worth several hundred pounds.

The Junto's members first tried keeping their books together in one room, but the volumes were inconvenient to use, and the collection fell apart. In 1731 Franklin proposed a library paid for by subscription, and with Brockden's help he drew up the articles, under which fifty people paid forty shillings to begin and ten shillings a year. This Library Company, he later wrote, became the mother of all the subscription libraries in North America, which are now so numerous.

When Franklin went from door to door seeking subscribers, he did not present the library as his own idea but as the wish of a number of friends who had asked him to approach those who loved reading. The plan went forward more smoothly, and he used the same method ever afterwards, recommending it warmly to anyone who wished to do good. If it stays uncertain for a while who deserves the credit, he explained, someone vainer than you will claim it, and then even envy will help to restore it to its rightful owner.

The library gave Franklin the means of constant study, and he set aside an hour or two every day to read, a habit that partly made up for the schooling he had missed. He believed that the subscription libraries that followed the first one had improved the conversation of the Americans and made common tradesmen and farmers as intelligent as most gentlemen in other countries. Perhaps, he added, they had even helped to give the colonies the courage to defend their rights.

Having more time for study, Franklin applied himself to languages, and he taught himself French first and then went on to Italian and Spanish. A friend who was also learning Italian often played chess with him, and the winner of each game could set the loser a task, such as learning a passage by heart. Each had to finish the task honestly before the next meeting, and the two friends improved quickly under this cheerful pressure.

When Franklin looked at Latin again, after his work on French, Italian and Spanish, he was surprised to find that he could read it with little trouble. This made him suspect that the usual method of teaching languages is backward, and that pupils would learn faster if they began with a modern language and then moved step by step toward the ancient ones. He added that even if a student did not go on to Latin, the time spent on the modern languages would not be wasted.

Around 1733, after about ten years away, Franklin travelled to Boston to see his family, and on the way he visited his brother James at Newport. James was in poor health, and the old anger between them melted away, and the sick man asked Benjamin to take his ten-year-old son and raise him as a printer. Franklin agreed, sent the boy to school and later took him into his own shop, hoping in this way to repay the years of service that he had taken from his brother by leaving.

In 1736 Franklin lost one of his sons, a fine boy of four years old named Francis, to smallpox, which the child had caught in the ordinary way. For a long time he bitterly regretted that he had not protected the boy by inoculation, and he never forgot the grief. He told the story for the sake of other parents, because his example showed that the regret may be the same whichever choice is made, and that the safer choice should therefore be preferred.

In 1732 Franklin published the first of his Almanacks, writing as an imaginary author called Richard Saunders, and he continued the series for about twenty-five years. He tried to make it both entertaining and useful, with jokes, weather predictions and wise sayings in the empty spaces between the days of the calendar. The book was in such demand that he sold nearly ten thousand copies every year, and it brought him a considerable profit.

In the little gaps between the important days of the calendar, Franklin printed proverbs that urged readers to practise hard work and thrift, as the road to wealth and, through wealth, to honest living. A man in want, he argued, finds it harder to act honestly, and to prove it he offered the saying that it is hard for an empty sack to stand upright. Poor Richard also offered such advice as early to bed and early to rise, and these short lines were soon quoted in homes and shops across the colonies.

Poor Richard played a famous joke on Titan Leeds, a rival Almanack maker, by predicting that Leeds would die on a particular day in October 1733. When Leeds angrily replied that he was still alive, Poor Richard answered with perfect politeness that the dead man's ghost must be writing the paper, since the real Leeds had surely died at the hour named. The joke amused readers for years, and it did Poor Richard no harm at all.

For the Almanack of 1758, Franklin gathered all the scattered sayings of Poor Richard into one connected speech, given by a wise old man to the crowd at an auction. Bringing the advice together in this way gave it far greater force, and the piece was copied in all the newspapers of the continent and printed on a sheet in Britain to be hung on walls. It was even translated twice into French, and many clergymen and gentlemen bought copies to give to their poorer neighbours.

Brought up as a Presbyterian, Franklin held a few simple beliefs which he thought were the essentials of every religion, and the first was that God made the world and governs it by His providence. He believed that the most acceptable service to God was to do good to other people, that our souls are immortal, and that all crimes will be punished and all virtue rewarded, either in this life or the next. He did not often attend public worship, but he paid every year toward the support of the Presbyterian minister, since he thought religion useful to the community.

A young Presbyterian preacher from Ireland named Samuel Hemphill began to preach in Philadelphia, and his sermons dealt chiefly with moral virtue rather than with the finer points of doctrine. Franklin liked this teaching and became one of his warm supporters, writing two or three pamphlets in his defence against the church leaders who wished to remove him. When an opponent proved that one of Hemphill's best sermons had been copied from a British writer, Franklin gave up the cause, and he stopped attending church and used his Sundays for study.

Many years later two friends, Abel James and Benjamin Vaughan, wrote to urge Franklin to continue his memoirs, which they believed would be an instructive example to the young. In 1784 he was living at Passy, near Paris, where he served his new nation as its envoy, and after a long interruption he resumed the narrative. The pages that follow were composed in France, and they describe an ambitious scheme, conceived long before, to improve his own character.

Around this time Franklin conceived the bold and difficult project of arriving at moral perfection, and he wished to live without committing any fault at any time. He thought that, since he knew what was right and what was wrong, he could surely always do the one and avoid the other, but he soon discovered that the task was harder than he had imagined. While he was guarding against one fault he was often surprised by another, because habit took advantage of any lapse of attention, and inclination was sometimes stronger than reason.

Franklin concluded that the mere wish to be perfect would not protect him, and that good habits had to be built before good conduct could be relied on. He therefore listed the virtues that seemed to him necessary, among them temperance, silence, order, resolution, frugality, industry, sincerity and justice, and he wrote beside each one a short rule that explained its meaning. The rest were moderation, cleanliness, tranquillity and chastity, and he arranged the whole list so that mastering the earlier virtues would make the later ones easier.

Franklin made a little book with a page for each virtue, ruled in red ink into seven columns for the days of the week and crossed by lines for the virtues. Every evening he marked a black spot in the proper place for each fault that he found upon examination, and he gave one week of strict attention to each virtue in turn. In this way he could pass through the whole list in thirteen weeks and repeat the course four times in a year, as a gardener clears one bed at a time.

Franklin began each day by asking himself what good he would do, and he ended it by asking what good he had done. He rose at five, washed and offered a short prayer, planned the day's business and then worked in his shop until noon, with a break for reading and breakfast. In the evening he put things in their places, took supper with music or conversation, and examined his day before he went to bed at ten.

Temperance came first on Franklin's list, because it brings coolness and clearness of head, which are needed when one must keep constant watch against old habits. Silence came next, since he wished to gain knowledge, and he judged that knowledge is gained in conversation rather by the ears than by the tongue. He therefore tried to break a habit of prattling, punning and joking, which had made him welcome only to trifling company.

Of all the virtues, Order gave Franklin the most trouble, and his papers and his hours refused to stay where he put them, however often he tried. He compared himself to a man who bought an axe from a smith and asked to have the whole blade made as bright as the edge. After turning the wheel for a time, the weary customer gave up and took the axe as it was, saying that he thought he liked a speckled axe best.

Beside each virtue Franklin wrote a short rule, and the rules for resolution, frugality and industry were among the plainest, telling him to perform without fail what he resolved, to waste nothing and to lose no time. Sincerity, justice, moderation, cleanliness and tranquillity were guarded by similar rules, which told him to use no hurtful deceit, to wrong no one and to avoid extremes. He believed that frugality and industry, once they had freed him from debt, would bring him independence and make it easier to practise sincerity and justice.

His list at first contained only twelve virtues, but a Quaker friend kindly told him that people thought him proud, and that he often seemed overbearing in conversation, and so he added humility as a thirteenth. The rule that he wrote beside it was to imitate Jesus and Socrates, and he made it a law to avoid directly contradicting others or stating his own opinions with any air of certainty. Instead of saying certainly or undoubtedly, he used words like I conceive, I apprehend or it appears to me at present.

Franklin wrote that of all our natural passions pride is perhaps the hardest to subdue, because however much one hides or struggles against it, it is still alive and will peep out now and then. He even joked that if he ever believed that he had conquered it completely, he would probably be proud of his humility. Yet the modest manner he practised helped him greatly, for although he was a poor speaker, hesitant and often incorrect, he usually carried his points.

Franklin admitted that he never arrived at the perfection he had so ambitiously sought, but the attempt made him a better and a happier man than he would otherwise have been. He credited temperance for his long and steady health, industry and frugality for his early comfort and his knowledge, and sincerity and justice for the trust that his country placed in him. He hoped that some of his descendants would follow the example and share the rewards.

Franklin planned to write a book called The Art of Virtue, which would show the advantages of each virtue and the harm of its opposite vice, and so explain how to become good. He thought that wrong actions are not harmful because they are forbidden, but are forbidden because they are harmful, and that anyone who understood this should want to avoid them. He also dreamed of a united party of good people from every nation, but the pressure of public and private business always prevented him from completing either project.

Franklin carefully excluded libel and personal abuse from his newspaper, even when writers claimed that a newspaper was like a stagecoach in which anyone who paid had a right to a seat. He offered to print the piece separately for the author to distribute, but he would not spread its attacks to readers who had paid for something useful or entertaining. He also explained, in a famous essay of 1731, that printers believe both sides of a dispute deserve a hearing, and that truth will beat error when each has fair play.

Franklin helped several of his workmen to open print shops in other colonies, supplying the press and type in return for a third of the profits for six years. In Charleston, South Carolina, one partner died, and his widow, who had been born and brought up in Holland, where girls learned accounting, sent Franklin a clear statement of the past and an exact account every quarter afterwards. She managed the business so well that she raised her family respectably, and when the term ended she bought the printing house from him and established her son in it.

In 1736 Franklin was chosen to be the clerk of the General Assembly of Pennsylvania, a post to which he was re-elected each year for several years. The pay was useful, but the place also gave him a chance to keep up friendships among the members, who then gave him the profitable work of printing the votes, laws and paper money of the colony. One year a new member, a gentleman of fortune and education, made a long speech against him, and Franklin felt uneasy, for the man was clearly likely to gain great influence.

Rather than flatter the new member, Franklin wrote him a note saying that he had heard of a very scarce and curious book in his library and asking to borrow it for a few days. The book was sent at once, and Franklin returned it a week later with a second note that thanked him warmly, after which the member spoke to him in the Assembly with great civility. They became firm friends until the man's death, and Franklin took it as proof of the old saying that one who has done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another than one you have obliged yourself.

In 1737 Colonel Spotswood, who was then the postmaster-general, was displeased with the way his deputy in Philadelphia kept his accounts, and he took the post from him and offered it to Franklin.
