Franklin accepted gladly, for although the salary was small, the office made it easier to gather news and to send out his paper, so that his newspaper sold better and attracted more advertisements. In time the position produced a considerable income, and it made Franklin better known to leading people throughout the colonies.

Franklin remembered that when Andrew Bradford had been postmaster, he had forbidden the post riders to carry Franklin's newspaper, and Franklin had been obliged to bribe them to take it secretly. He had thought this conduct mean, and so, when the office came to him, he refused to copy it, and Bradford's paper travelled in the mail on the same terms as his own. Because Bradford held the post, people had thought his paper better placed to gather news and to carry advertisements, and Franklin's own paper had suffered from that advantage.

In 1739 a famous travelling preacher named George Whitefield arrived in Philadelphia, and when the local clergy refused him their pulpits he spoke in the open air to enormous crowds of every sect and denomination. Franklin, who was one of his hearers, was struck by the extraordinary power of his oratory, and by the way in which people admired him even when he told them that they were by nature half beasts and half devils. The change in the town was remarkable, for one could not walk through the streets in the evening without hearing psalms sung in the houses on every side.

Whitefield had a loud, clear voice and spoke so perfectly that he could be heard at a great distance, and Franklin, who stood among the hindmost listeners one evening, decided to find out how far. He walked backward down Market Street toward the river until the preacher's voice began to fade near Front Street, and then he imagined a half circle with that distance as its radius, filled with people standing two square feet apiece. He calculated that more than thirty thousand people might hear a single speaker, and that made the old stories of generals addressing whole armies seem believable to him.

Franklin disagreed with Whitefield's plan to build an orphan house in Georgia, and when he sensed that a collection was coming at the end of one sermon, he silently resolved that he would give nothing. He had a handful of copper coins, three or four silver dollars and five gold pistoles in his pocket, and as the preacher continued he began to soften and decided to give the coppers. Another stroke of oratory made him ashamed of that, so he determined to give the silver, and by the end of the sermon he had emptied his whole pocket, gold and all, into the collector's dish.

When Whitefield returned to Philadelphia, Franklin offered him a bed in his house, and the preacher replied that if he did so for Christ's sake, he would not miss his reward. Franklin answered quickly that he had made the offer not for Christ's sake, but for Whitefield's own. The preacher sometimes prayed for his host's conversion, and he never had the satisfaction of seeing it, but theirs was a sincere civil friendship that lasted until Whitefield died.

Whitefield wished to build his orphan house in Georgia, but Franklin believed it would be wiser to build it in Philadelphia, because in Georgia both materials and workmen had to be brought at great expense. He gave this advice plainly, and when the preacher rejected it obstinately, Franklin refused to contribute, although he still admired the man himself. Franklin also printed many of Whitefield's sermons and journals, and the sales made the preacher's name even better known.

Franklin observed that Whitefield's delivery improved with repetition, until every accent, every emphasis and every change of tone was so perfectly placed that one could enjoy the discourse without caring about its subject. It was a pleasure much like that of hearing an excellent piece of music, and it gave travelling preachers an advantage over those who stayed in one pulpit and could not rehearse so often. The printed sermons read less well than they sounded, which Franklin took as a reminder that a speaker's manner can carry what a page cannot.

In a newspaper letter of 1735 Franklin pointed out that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and soon afterward he proposed forming a company for putting out fires and for saving goods from houses in danger. Thirty men joined, and each promised to keep a certain number of leather buckets, strong bags and baskets in good order and to bring them to every fire. They met once a month for a social evening to talk over ideas about fire fighting, and the Union Fire Company, as it was called, was still flourishing when Franklin wrote about it fifty years later.

The Union Fire Company proved so useful that so many men wished to join it that others formed companies of their own, one after another, until they included most of the men of property in the town. In 1752 Franklin and other members of his company went a step further and founded the Philadelphia Contributionship, which insured houses against loss by fire. Both ideas showed his belief that neighbours can protect one another better when they work together.

Franklin disliked the city watch, for householders were supposed to take turns at night duty, but the constables let them off for a yearly fee of six shillings, which was often spent on drink. The watch was therefore a small band of idle men, and the fee was unfair too, since a poor widow paid as much as a rich merchant with a warehouse full of goods. He wrote a paper for the Junto proposing that watchmen should be paid and that the cost should be raised by a tax in proportion to each person's property.

The Junto approved the plan for a paid watch, and Franklin shared it with several other clubs that had been formed by the Junto's friends, so that each could appear to propose it as its own idea. In this way public opinion was prepared without any one man seeming to push, and the proposal was adopted into law a few years afterward. Franklin had learned that a good plan travels farther when many people feel that they own it.

In those days the streets of Philadelphia were unpaved, and in wet weather the market was a quagmire in which heavy wagons sank and shoppers waded through mud. Franklin persuaded some neighbours to pay for the paving of one part of the market place with stone, and the improvement was gratefully received. Soon, however, the carts that came from the unpaved lanes brought mud onto the new stones, and the street was almost as dirty as before.

Franklin found a poor but industrious man who was willing to sweep the pavement before the neighbours' doors regularly for sixpence a month from each household. He then wrote and printed a paper showing how cheap the plan was, and how much dirt and dust would be kept out of shops and houses where it spoiled the goods. People tried the plan, found that it worked, and it was later extended by law to the whole city.

The street lamps first used in Philadelphia were globes imported from London, and they were blackened by smoke within a few hours, so that they gave very little light. Franklin designed a lamp of four flat panes of glass with a long funnel above to draw up the smoke and little crevices below to let in the air, and these lamps burned bright until morning. If a stray blow broke a pane, it could be replaced quickly and cheaply, which was another advantage over the globe lamps.

Franklin admitted that some readers might think such matters as dust and street lamps too small to mention, but he reminded them that a small trouble repeated in a crowded city becomes a great one. Human happiness, he wrote, is produced not so much by great pieces of good fortune that seldom happen as by little advantages that occur every day. He added that if you teach a poor young man to shave himself and keep his razor in order, you may do more for his happiness than if you gave him a thousand guineas.

In 1743 Franklin thought that the British colonies had at last gained enough leisure to turn their attention to science, and he drew up a plan for a society of curious people who would share their discoveries. He proposed that it should be called the American Philosophical Society, and he served as its first secretary, writing to members in the other colonies and gathering their reports. It faded after only a few years, but it was revived later, and it still exists today.

In 1742 Franklin invented an open iron stove that warmed a room much better than a common fireplace, and it saved fuel because the fresh air that entered was warmed on its way in. His old friend Robert Grace, who owned an iron furnace, cast the plates for these stoves as the demand grew, and Franklin wrote a pamphlet to explain them. Governor Thomas offered him a patent for the sole right to sell the stoves, but Franklin refused, saying that since we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should serve others by any invention of ours.

When war broke out between Britain and France and Spain in the 1740s, enemy ships began to threaten the Delaware River, and Philadelphia had no forts, no guns and no soldiers. The Assembly, in which Quakers held the majority, would not vote money for war because their religion forbade it, and the governor, who wanted a defence, quarrelled with them year after year. Franklin saw that the city was in real danger, and he decided that something must be done.

Franklin wrote and published a pamphlet called Plain Truth, in which he described the defenceless state of the colony in the strongest terms and argued that union and discipline were needed for its defence. He promised that within a few days he would propose an association, which everyone might sign, for that very purpose. The pamphlet had a sudden and surprising effect, and the whole town began to discuss it.

Franklin called a meeting of the citizens at the New Building, a large hall in the town, and he had prepared printed copies of the paper with pens and ink spread around the room. After a short speech he handed out the copies, which were eagerly signed without a single objection, and more than twelve hundred people had signed before the meeting broke up. Copies sent into the countryside brought the number of signers to over ten thousand, and they bought weapons, formed companies and regiments and met every week for drill.

The Philadelphia regiment elected Franklin as its colonel, but he believed himself unfit for the post and declined it, recommending instead a Mr Lawrence, a fine person and a man of influence. Lawrence was appointed, and Franklin, content to work behind the scenes, proposed a lottery to pay for a battery of guns below the town. The tickets sold so quickly that the work soon began, and the walls of the battery were framed of logs and filled with earth.

Franklin and three other men were sent to New York to borrow cannon from Governor Clinton, who at first refused them flatly. At dinner with his council, where a great deal of Madeira wine was drunk, as the custom of the place then was, he softened by degrees and said that he would lend six. After a few more glasses he raised the number to ten, and at last he good-naturedly agreed to lend eighteen.

The cannon were splendid eighteen-pounders, and they were soon carried to the town's battery on their carriages and mounted in their places. The volunteers kept a guard there every night as long as the war lasted, and Franklin regularly took his turn of duty as a common soldier. The battery, whose walls were framed of logs and filled with earth, had been paid for by the lottery that Franklin had proposed.

The companies asked Franklin to supply devices and mottoes for their flags, and he did so with great cheerfulness, adding colour and spirit to the new movement. The Governor and his council were glad to see the colony defended, and they treated him with respect for a time. Thomas Penn, however, one of the Proprietors of the colony, resented the whole business, and he began to think of Franklin as a man who had too much influence over the people.

Peace came in 1748, and the Association, which had served its purpose, gradually faded away, though the guns still stood in the battery by the river. The whole episode had shown that ordinary citizens can unite to protect themselves when a divided government will not act. It also made Franklin a leader whom the people trusted, and a man whom the Proprietors began to watch with suspicion.

The governor put Franklin into the commission of the peace, which made him a local judge, and for a short time he attended the courts. He soon found that the work required more knowledge of the common law than he possessed, and he did not wish to act in that station without credit. He therefore withdrew gradually, excusing himself on the ground that his duties as a lawmaker in the Assembly demanded all his attention.

In 1748 Franklin took into partnership David Hall, a skilled and honest workman who had served him well, and Hall relieved him of all care of the printing house while paying him his share of the profits punctually. The partnership lasted eighteen years and was successful for both men, and it gave Franklin the leisure that he had long wished for. Believing that he had gained a tolerable competency, he flattered himself that he could now take his ease and give his time to philosophical studies and amusements.

In 1746, while visiting Boston, Franklin met a Dr Spence, who had recently arrived from Scotland and who showed him some experiments in electricity. They were imperfectly performed, since the doctor was not very expert, but the subject was quite new to Franklin, and the sparks and shocks both surprised and delighted him. He was soon eager to learn more about this mysterious force, which few people in the colonies had ever seen.

Soon after Franklin returned to Philadelphia, the Library Company received from Peter Collinson of London a gift of a glass tube, together with an account of how it might be used for electrical experiments. Franklin seized the chance to repeat what he had seen in Boston, and by much practice he became skilful at those described from England too, adding a number of new ones of his own. His house was soon full of people who had come to see these new wonders, and he was glad to share the work.

To share the burden of showing the experiments, Franklin had several glass tubes blown at the local glasshouse and gave them to his friends, so that he soon had a team of performers. The best of them was Ebenezer Kinnersley, an ingenious neighbour who was out of work, and Franklin encouraged him to lecture for money and wrote two lectures in which each experiment helped the audience to understand the next. Kinnersley's talks were well attended, and after a time he toured the colonies, showing the wonders in every large town.

Franklin loved to mix play with science, and in a letter of 1749 he described, with a straight face, a picnic planned for the banks of the Schuylkill River. A turkey, he wrote, was to be killed for the dinner by an electric shock and roasted on a spit turned by electricity, before a fire lit by an electrified bottle. The healths of the famous electricians of Europe were to be drunk in glasses that gave their lips a tingling shock.

In his experiments Franklin found that electricity behaves like a single fluid that can be present in excess, which he called positive, or in short supply, which he called negative. He also noticed that a pointed piece of metal draws off a spark silently and from a greater distance than a blunt one, and he began to suspect that lightning was nothing but a huge electric spark. If that were true, he reasoned, a tall iron rod with a sharp point might lead the lightning harmlessly into the ground and so protect buildings from fire.

At first the Royal Society in London thought Franklin's letters on electricity hardly worth printing, but his friend Collinson published them as a book, and a French translation soon attracted wide attention. In May 1752 near Paris, a scientist named Dalibard set up a tall iron rod during a thunderstorm exactly as Franklin had proposed, and he drew sparks from it, showing that lightning is electricity. The Royal Society, which had at first ignored his ideas, was later glad to honour him.

According to the most famous account, Franklin flew a kite during a thunderstorm near Philadelphia in June 1752, with a key tied to the wet string. When a spark jumped from the key to his knuckle, it showed him that the clouds really were full of electricity, and he urged people to protect their buildings with pointed iron rods. Franklin put one of the rods on his own house, and in time many buildings in the colonies and in Europe were guarded in the same way.

In 1753 the Royal Society of London gave Franklin its gold Copley medal for his electrical discoveries, and the colleges of Harvard and Yale each gave him an honorary degree of Master of Arts, though he had never attended college. He never took out a patent for the lightning rod or any other invention, keeping to his rule that he should be glad to serve others freely. Later the Royal Society went further and made him a Fellow without charging the usual fees.

In 1749 Franklin wrote a pamphlet called Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pennsylvania, and he gave copies free to the leading citizens, to prepare their minds. When he judged that they had read it, he began a subscription for opening and supporting an academy, with the money to be paid in yearly shares over five years, since he reckoned that the gift would then seem lighter. As in the matter of the library, he did not present himself as the author of the plan, but as one of a group of public-spirited gentlemen.

The new Academy opened in 1751 in the great hall that the citizens had built years before for Whitefield and other travelling preachers, and the trustees agreed to pay off its debt and to divide it into schoolrooms. Twenty-four trustees from different churches governed it, and Franklin wrote its constitution and served on the board for many years. The Academy grew steadily over the following decades, and in time it became the University of Pennsylvania, one of the great universities of America.

Dr Thomas Bond conceived the idea of a hospital in Philadelphia for the sick poor, a very kind design that was entirely his own, though people later credited it to Franklin. Bond worked hard to gather subscriptions, but the plan was new in America and badly understood, and he met with small success until he came to Franklin with a compliment. Whenever he proposed it to rich men, he said, they asked whether Franklin had been consulted, and when he admitted that he had not, they replied that they would think it over.

Franklin asked Bond to explain the plan carefully, and when he understood its usefulness he not only subscribed himself but threw himself into the work of gaining subscriptions from others. Before asking for money, he did what was his usual custom in such cases, which was to prepare the minds of the people by writing about the subject in the newspapers, a step that Bond had left out. The articles helped, but the gifts were still too few, and it was clear that more would be needed.

Many country members of the Assembly opposed spending public money on a city hospital, so Franklin proposed a bill that promised two thousand pounds, to be paid only when private citizens had raised the same sum by voluntary gifts. Those who disliked the project voted for the bill, believing that the condition could never be met, while those who liked it knew that the offer would double every private gift. Franklin wrote that he remembered no other political manoeuvre whose success gave him more pleasure, or in which he more easily excused himself for using a little cunning.

Subscriptions soon passed the sum that was needed, and the managers claimed the public gift, which enabled them to carry the design into execution. The Pennsylvania Hospital began to care for patients in a rented house in 1752, and in 1755 the cornerstone of its handsome new building was laid, with words that Franklin had composed asking God to bless the undertaking. The hospital proved useful from the start, and it still treats patients in Philadelphia today.

In 1751 the voters of Philadelphia chose Franklin as a member of the Assembly, and they went on re-electing him for many years afterward. Two years later, in 1753, he was appointed, together with a Mr William Hunter, as joint postmaster-general of the American colonies, with a salary to be paid out of the profits of the post. Franklin worked hard to make the post efficient, and in time it paid its way and began to bring a profit to the Crown.

In 1754, with war against France close at hand, the Lords of Trade ordered the colonies to send commissioners to Albany to confer with the chiefs of the Six Nations about the defence of the country. Franklin was named among the commissioners for Pennsylvania, and on the way he drew up a plan for uniting all the colonies under a single government for defence and other general purposes. In New York he showed it to two men of great knowledge in public affairs, James Alexander and Mr Kennedy, and with their approval he dared to lay it before the Congress.

In May 1754 Franklin printed in his Gazette a small picture of a snake cut into eight pieces, each labelled with the initials of a colony or a group of colonies. Beneath it he placed the stark words Join, or Die, which warned that the colonies would perish separately but might survive together. It is often called the first political cartoon in America, and it was copied in other newspapers throughout the colonies.

Franklin's plan provided for a general government to be run by a President General, appointed and supported by the Crown, and a Grand Council chosen by the elected assemblies of the several colonies. The debates went on day after day at Albany, side by side with the talks with the chiefs of the Six Nations, and many objections were raised before they were all overcome and the plan was agreed to. Copies were then sent to the Board of Trade in London and to the assemblies of the colonies.

The plan failed, for the assemblies of the colonies rejected it as giving too much power to the Crown, while the Crown rejected it as giving too much power to the people. Franklin suspected from these contrary reasons that it had been the true middle way, and he remained convinced that it would have been happy for both sides if it had been adopted. The colonies, so united, would have been strong enough to defend themselves, he thought, and the later quarrel over taxes and the bloody contest that followed might have been avoided.

The Assembly's dispute with Governor Morris was a bitter one, for the governor was bound by the Proprietors' instructions never to let their estates be taxed, while the Assembly thought that everyone should share the cost of defence. Franklin was often the one who drew up the Assembly's replies to the governor's messages, and the two sides exchanged many sharp words in public. Yet Morris was a lively and agreeable man who enjoyed an argument, and he bore Franklin no ill will, even inviting him to dine at his table.

In the spring of 1755 General Braddock arrived in Virginia with two regiments of British soldiers, planning to march into the western wilderness and capture the French fort at Fort Duquesne. He was waiting at Frederick, in Maryland, for wagons that had been promised, and he was angry with the Pennsylvania Assembly for not having given him more help. The Assembly sent Franklin, ostensibly on post office business, to smooth matters over, and he rode to the camp with his son William.

Braddock complained that Virginia and Maryland had provided only a handful of wagons fit for use, and Franklin remarked that it was a pity he had not landed in Pennsylvania, where almost every farmer owned a wagon. The general eagerly seized on the words and begged Franklin, as a man with influence there, to find the wagons himself. Franklin wrote down the terms that seemed necessary, the general agreed to them, and a commission and instructions were prepared on the spot.

At Lancaster, Franklin published a notice that a hundred and fifty wagons with four horses each, and fifteen hundred pack horses, were wanted for the king's forces, and he offered good daily pay for each of them. He added a shrewd warning that, if the farmers would not hire them out, Sir John St Clair, a stern officer, might come with soldiers and take them by force. The farmers believed Franklin's word, because they trusted him and knew that he was truly their friend.

The farmers did not trust the army's promises, so Franklin pledged his own bond that they would be paid, and the owners came forward in large numbers. He advanced money from the funds that Braddock had given him, and when that sum proved too small he added more of his own. In about two weeks a hundred and fifty wagons, with two hundred and fifty-nine horses to carry loads, were on their way to the camp.

Franklin learned that the junior officers of the army were poor and had little money to buy necessities for the long march, so he persuaded a committee of the Assembly to pay for a gift. He bought twenty parcels, each containing such things as sugar, tea, coffee, chocolate, biscuit, cheese, butter, hams and wine, and each parcel was loaded on a horse, which was also a gift to the officer who received it. His son William, who understood camp life, led the little train to the army, and Braddock wrote a warm letter of thanks and repaid Franklin's money.

Braddock expected to reach Fort Duquesne in a few days, but Franklin, who had his doubts, warned him that the army's line of march, nearly four miles long, might be cut like a thread by a surprise attack. The general smiled at his ignorance and replied that such enemies might endanger raw American militia but could make no impression on the King's trained regulars. Knowing that it was improper for a printer to argue with a soldier about his own profession, Franklin said no more.

On 9 July 1755, only a few miles from Fort Duquesne, Braddock's army was ambushed by French soldiers and their Native allies firing from the trees, just as Franklin had feared. The British regulars were thrown into confusion, and the general was mortally wounded and died a few days later, while the survivors fled in disorder. The army's second commander, Colonel Dunbar, destroyed much of the stores and hurried the troops back toward Philadelphia, leaving the frontier open.

After the disaster, the owners of the lost wagons and horses came to Franklin and demanded payment, as his bond required, and the claims were so large that he knew he could never pay them from his own purse. He was greatly perplexed, and for a time he feared that he would be ruined by the very service he had done for the army. In the end General Shirley, who had taken command, appointed commissioners to examine the claims, and most of them were paid out of the army's funds, to Franklin's great relief.

With the frontier exposed, Franklin drew a bill for establishing and training a voluntary militia, and it passed the Assembly without much difficulty, because care was taken to leave the Quakers at liberty. To encourage people to join, he also wrote and printed a dialogue that stated every objection to such a militia that he could imagine and answered each of them in turn. He thought that the dialogue had a great effect on the public, and that it helped many men to make up their minds.

In the winter of 1755 raiding parties attacked farms and villages along the Pennsylvania frontier, and the Moravian mission at Gnadenhutten was destroyed. Governor Morris asked Franklin to take charge of the defence of the north-west frontier and to build a line of forts, and Franklin, who had little confidence in his own military abilities, nevertheless accepted the task. He was given a commission and a bundle of blank ones for officers, and he soon raised about five hundred and sixty men, with his son William as his aide.

Franklin marched first to Bethlehem, the chief settlement of the Moravians, and found it in a good posture of defence, for the destruction of their mission at Gnadenhutten had made them fear for their lives. The principal buildings were protected by a stockade, and the town had bought a quantity of arms and ammunition from New York. They had even placed small paving stones between the windows of their tall stone houses, so that the women might throw them down on the heads of any attackers who tried to force their way in.

At Gnadenhutten, Franklin's men felled tall pine trees with their axes and set them upright in the ground to form a stockade, which became Fort Allen. They had only one small swivel gun, which they mounted at a corner and fired from time to time to let the enemy know that they had such pieces. Franklin called it a miserable stockade, but it was finished in about a week, although it rained so hard every other day that the men could not work.

Franklin noticed that the men were cheerful and good-natured when they were busy, and quarrelsome when it rained and they had nothing to do. The chaplain, Mr Beatty, complained that the men did not attend his prayers, although they never failed to come for their daily gill of rum. Franklin told him that it might be below his dignity to deal out the rum, but that if he did so just after prayers he would have every man about him, and never were prayers more punctually attended.

When an experienced officer, Colonel Clapham, arrived at the new forts, Franklin read his own commission to the garrison, recommended Clapham as a man of experience and handed over the command. He rode back to Philadelphia, where the volunteer regiment had elected him its colonel, and its mounted officers met him with drawn swords and escorted him home. Franklin thought the honour excessive, but it greatly offended the friends of the Proprietors, who said that such a compliment had been paid only to the governor.

Governor Denny arrived from England in August 1756 with the gold medal that the Royal Society had voted to Franklin, and he presented it with compliments at a public dinner. Afterwards he took Franklin aside and hinted that the Proprietors would reward him handsomely if he would support the governor's measures and stop opposing their interests. Franklin answered that he needed no favours, and that, as a member of the Assembly, he could not accept any without being bribed, although he would gladly serve the Proprietors whenever their measures were good for the public.

The quarrel over taxing the Proprietors' estates went on for months, until the Assembly decided to petition the King and chose Franklin as its agent to carry the complaint to London. The task was a hard and uncertain one, because he would have to argue against the powerful Penn family before the king's ministers. Franklin accepted, put his business and papers in order, and prepared to leave his family.

In the spring of 1757 Franklin travelled to New York to take passage on the mail ship that carried the dispatches of the commander-in-chief, Lord Loudoun, to England. Every time he inquired when the ship would sail, he was told that Loudoun's letters would be ready the next day, and the next day always brought a new delay. The passengers who were eager to cross the ocean, Franklin among them, could do nothing but wait for weeks.

In the general's waiting room Franklin met a messenger named Innis, who had come from Philadelphia and had been kept waiting for some weeks for his answers. Innis explained, with a bitter smile, that Lord Loudoun was like the figure of St George on the tavern signs, who is always on horseback and never rides on. Franklin saw that a commander who could not make up his mind about a few letters was hardly likely to move an army quickly.

At last, in June 1757, Franklin's ship sailed from New York for England, carrying the general's dispatches and a number of anxious passengers. Near the end of the voyage, in darkness and thick weather, the vessel passed dangerously close to the rocks off the south-west coast of England, and the passengers were lucky to escape. In July 1757, Franklin landed at Falmouth, and from there he made his way toward London, where his long work as a public man in Europe was to begin.

Franklin wrote his life story in several parts, at different times, and he died in 1790 at the age of eighty-four without carrying it any further than the year 1757. In the years that followed he would help to shape a new nation, serving as a scientist, a diplomat and a leader in the founding of the United States. Yet the little book he left us still shows what its author valued most, which was curiosity, hard work, honesty and a determination to make himself and the world a little better.
